Rhapsody can answer questions about itself. The assistant searches the documentation that ships inside the framework package, shows you the sections that match, and, during development with an API key, writes a short answer that points back to the pages it used. It is meant to shorten the learning curve of a new framework: instead of hunting through the docs, you ask in plain English and get the page that explains it.

Optional and development-only. Searching the docs from the terminal needs no API key and no network. Written AI answers and the browser page only run when `app_env` is `development`. Nothing here is active in production.

```bash
php rhapsody ask "what does the ask command do"
```

With no API key, the command prints the best matching documentation sections, with code samples, followed by a `Sources:` list of the pages they came from. With a key (in development), you first get a short answer that cites those sections as `[1]`, `[2]`, and so on, and the sources it used are marked cited.

```text
Answer text that cites the sections it used [1].

Sources:
  [1] Page › Section heading - /docs/page (cited)
  [2] Another page › Another section - /docs/another-page
```

Option | What it does
`--no-ai` | Never call the model, even in development with a key. Just show the matching sections.
`--top=N` | How many sections to retrieve, from 1 to 10. The default is 4.
`--json` | Print the result as JSON (question, answer, notices, and every source with its score and text), for scripts and editors.

1. Search. Your question is matched against a search index of the Rhapsody documentation that ships with `arout/rhapsody-core`. It is a plain keyword search (BM25) that runs locally in PHP: it understands class names such as `SchemaOrg`, method names, and `snake_case` or `camelCase` words, and it weights headings above body text.
2. Answer (optional). In development, with an API key, the top sections are sent to the model with an instruction to answer only from them and to cite each claim as `[n]`.
3. Check. If the answer cites a section that was never provided, or cites nothing at all, it is thrown away and you get the sections instead. If the model says the sections do not contain the answer, you are told the docs may not cover it.
4. Sources. The pages used are always listed, so you can verify any answer against the documentation.

headingPath: If anything fails, you still get the docs
chunks.text: A missing or rejected key, a rate limit, a timeout, a provider outage, a blocked or empty reply: each one produces a one-line notice and the matching documentation sections. The assistant never fails just because the AI is unavailable.

When the search finds only a weak match, or the model reports that the docs do not cover a question, the question is appended to `storage/logs/doc-gaps.jsonl` with the best page found and its score. Each line is one JSON object, so the file shows where the documentation needs work.

For `ask`, only your question and the text of public documentation sections are sent to the model. No request data, headers, session, environment values, or application code are included. The toolbar and error page helpers below are different: they send a masked picture of one request, and the error page also sends a few lines of your source code. They always show you that text first.

Two development tools use the AI client on the request you are looking at, built on the request snapshots:

- Ask AI, a tab in the debug toolbar. Ask a question about the page you just loaded, such as why it was slow or whether it ran N+1 queries.
- Explain and fix, a button on the error page. It explains why the request failed and can propose a change to your code.

Both are development-only and need a working AI client (see Setup below). Neither is active in production, and both can be switched off in config.

Clicking Review and ask (or Review and explain) sends nothing to the AI provider. It builds the message on your server and shows it to you: a list of sections with their sizes, the source files included, and the exact text under Show the exact text. Untick a section and the text updates. Only Send sends it. In the toolbar you can tick Do not show this review again in this browser session; the error page, which sends source code, always shows it.

Every message that is sent is also recorded in `storage/logs/ai-requests.jsonl` (time, mode, snapshot id, which sections, which source files, size, provider), so you can always check afterwards what left your machine.

headingPath: Ask AI and Explain and fix
chunks.text:
- Toolbar, Ask AI: your question plus the request snapshot: method, URL, query and body, matched route, status, time and memory, database queries and N+1 findings, cache statistics and the middleware trace. Logs, environment values, container services, request headers and session keys are available but off until you tick them. The client IP is never included.
- Error page, Explain and fix: the exception (class, message, stack trace), the request and route, recent log lines, allowlisted environment values, and up to three source excerpts of about 30 lines around the failing lines.
- Masked first. Everything passes through the snapshot redactor: values under keys such as `password`, `token` or `api_key`, bearer tokens, JWTs, URL credentials and well-known key formats are replaced by `[REDACTED]`. In source code, string literals assigned to such names ( `'api_key' => '...'`, `$password = '...'`, `define('X_SECRET', '...')`) are masked too.
- Never read: `.env` files, `config/`, `storage/`, `.git/`, `node_modules/`, files outside the project and anything that is not a source file (php, twig, js, ts, css, scss, html).

The message tells the model that everything in it (SQL, headers, log lines, exception messages, code comments) is untrusted data, not instructions. The model can only reply with text; it never runs anything.

Rhapsody provides a complete, self-contained authentication system built with Doctrine ORM and the `User` entity. It handles registration, login, logout, and password reset flows out of the box.

Important:

The authentication system is optional. You are not required to use it. You can build your own authentication system, or extend the built-in one.

Before using the authentication system, you must create the required database tables. Run the following command from your project root:

```bash
php rhapsody auth:install
```

This command creates the `users` and `password_resets` tables based on the core `User` entity definition.

⚠️ Important:

Running `auth:install` is required before any authentication routes will work. The command will skip tables that already exist, so it's safe to run multiple times.

The authentication system is self-contained within the core framework:

- Controller: `Rhapsody\Core\Controllers\AuthController`
- Entity: `Rhapsody\Core\Entities\User`
- Views: `@core/auth/*.twig` (login, register, forgot-password, reset-password)
- Routes: Registered automatically from the core routes file

The following routes are available out of the box:

```text
GET  /login              → Show login form
POST /login              → Handle login
GET  /register           → Show registration form
POST /register           → Handle registration
POST /logout             → Log out
GET  /forgot-password    → Show forgot password form
POST /forgot-password    → Send reset link
GET  /reset-password/{token} → Show reset password form
POST /reset-password     → Handle password reset
```

To use the default authentication system, simply ensure the routes are registered (they are automatically loaded from the core) and point your users to `/login` and `/register`. In your templates, you can check if a user is logged in using the `auth` global: ```twig {{% if auth.check %}} Welcome back, {{ auth.user.name }}! Logout {{% else %}} Login Register {{% endif %}} ``` Protect routes with the `auth` middleware: ```php Router::get('/dashboard', [DashboardController::class, 'index'])->middleware('auth'); ```

To override the default authentication views, create matching templates in your active theme:

```bash
views/themes/your-theme/auth/login.twig
views/themes/your-theme/auth/register.twig
views/themes/your-theme/auth/forgot-password.twig
views/themes/your-theme/auth/reset-password.twig
```

The framework will automatically use your theme's templates instead of the core ones if you have set up your own theme; otherwise make sure that your view files extend `@core/layouts/main.twig`. See the themes documentation for more details on using core and custom themes.

The built-in authentication system includes the following security measures:

- Password hashing: Passwords are hashed using `password_hash()` with BCRYPT
- CSRF protection: All forms include a CSRF token field
- Session regeneration: Session ID is regenerated on login
- Password reset tokens: Tokens are hashed at rest (SHA-256) and time-limited (60 minutes)
- No user enumeration: Password reset responses are identical whether or not the email exists
- Single-use tokens: Reset tokens are deleted after successful use
- Old token invalidation: Requesting a new reset link invalidates all previous tokens

Rhapsody is built for performance and includes a robust, multi-driver caching system. This allows you to store the results of expensive operations, such as complex database queries or external API calls, to significantly speed up your application.

The framework supports multiple cache backends, or "drivers." You can switch between them with a single configuration change, allowing you to use a simple file-based cache locally and a high-performance Redis cache in production.

The driver is configured in your `.env` file:

```bash
# Use the local filesystem for caching
CACHE_DRIVER=file

# Use a Redis server for caching
CACHE_DRIVER=redis
```

When using the `redis` driver, you must also provide the connection details for your Redis server in your `.env` file.

```bash
REDIS_HOST=127.0.0.1
REDIS_PORT=6379
REDIS_PASSWORD=null
```
The cache is managed by the `Rhapsody\Core\Cache` class, which is available via the service container. The most common way to interact with the cache is the `remember()` method.

- `$this->cache->get('key')`: Retrieve an item from the cache.
- `$this->cache->put('key', $value, $minutes)`: Store an item in the cache.
- `$this->cache->has('key')`: Check if an item exists in the cache.
- `$this->cache->forget('key')`: Remove an item from the cache.

The built-in file and Redis drivers store values as JSON, so cache arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and `null`. Objects come back as associative arrays, not instances. The Redis driver throws a `JsonException` from `put()` if a value can't be JSON-encoded, rather than silently storing nothing.

Twig compiles templates the first time they are rendered. In production, you can pre‑compile all templates to eliminate the first‑visit delay. Use the CLI command:

```bash
php rhapsody app:cache-warm
```

The command walks through every Twig file in your active theme (and the default theme) and forces Twig to compile each one. It respects the theme fallback system, so templates that exist only in the default theme are also compiled.

Run this command after clearing caches or after deploying new template files to ensure optimal performance.

Rhapsody includes a powerful command-line interface built on the Symfony Console component. It is the primary tool for interacting with your application outside of the web browser, allowing you to automate tasks, generate boilerplate code, and manage your application's state.

The CLI is accessed via the `rhapsody` executable file in your project root.

To see a list of all available commands, simply run the application without any arguments. This will display a list of commands along with their descriptions.

```bash
php rhapsody
```

The console includes a suite of generator commands to quickly create new classes for your application. These commands create "stub" files in the correct directories, complete with the correct namespaces, base classes, and essential methods.

This command creates a new controller file in the `app/Controllers` directory.

```bash
php rhapsody make:controller OrderController
```

This will generate `app/Controllers/OrderController.php`.

This command creates a new model file in the `app/Models` directory.

```bash
php rhapsody make:model Order
```

This will generate `app/Models/Order.php`.

This command creates a new middleware file in the `app/Middleware` directory.

```bash
php rhapsody make:middleware CheckSubscriptionStatus
```

This will generate `app/Middleware/CheckSubscriptionStatusMiddleware.php`.
Migrations are like version control for your database. Rhapsody uses Phinx, managed through the console, to handle schema changes reliably across all development and production environments.

This command will create a new, timestamped migration file in the `db/migrations` directory. Use a descriptive name that explains what the migration does.

```bash
php rhapsody make:migration CreateProductsTable
```

To apply all pending migrations and update your database schema to the latest version, run the `migrate` command.

```bash
php rhapsody migrate
```
Rhapsody provides caching mechanisms to improve your application's performance in production. The console provides commands to manage these caches.

After clearing caches (or after a fresh deployment), the first visitor to a page may experience a slight delay because Twig compiles templates on the fly. To avoid this, you can pre‑compile all templates using the cache warmer.

```bash
php rhapsody app:cache-warm
```

The command scans both your active theme and the default theme, compiles every `.twig` file into the Twig cache directory. Subsequent requests will serve the pre‑compiled templates immediately.

By default, the command uses the direct compilation method. An alternative crawl method (which hits actual URLs) is also available for warming other caches (Doctrine, routes) – use `--method=crawl --base-url=https://yourdomain.com` if needed.

For a significant performance boost, you can compile all of your application's route definitions into a single, cached file.

```
# Generate the route cache file
php rhapsody route:cache

# Remove the route cache file (necessary after changing routes)
php rhapsody route:clear
```

Important: You must clear and re-cache your routes whenever you make a change to your `routes/web.php` or `routes/api.php` files.

Note: The `route:cache` command will fail if any of your routes use a closure as the callback. Always use controller/action pairs when you plan to cache routes.

This command will flush the entire application data cache, which is used by the `Rhapsody\Core\Cache` service.

```bash
php rhapsody cache:clear
```

This is useful during development when you've changed the underlying data that an expensive, cached operation depends on.

Rhapsody keeps all configuration in the `config/` directory and the `.env` file. You should never modify files inside the `/vendor` directory. This ensures that framework updates won't overwrite your customisations. Rhapsody is built with extensibility in mind; consult the documentation to learn how to extend or create custom functionality.

- `.env` – environment‑specific variables (database, mail, caching driver, etc.).
- `config.php` – general settings (middleware, theme, logging paths, etc.).

Golden Rule: If you need to change behaviour, look for a configuration file first. Only extend or replace classes – never edit core files directly.

You can create additional config files in the `config/` folder and load them in your controllers or services as needed. This is useful for tasks like defining constants or paths, or for custom modules you create. Your custom config files will never be touched when updating the framework.
The `.env` file contains sensitive or environment‑specific data. Never commit it to version control. Use `.env.example` as a template.

Environment variables are always strings, and PHP types `$_ENV` loosely. The `Rhapsody\Core\Support\Env` class reads a variable and converts it to the type you want, falling back to a default when the variable is unset (or can't be converted):

```php
use Rhapsody\Core\Support\Env;

$name    = Env::string('APP_NAME', 'Rhapsody');   // string
$timeout = Env::int('GEMINI_TIMEOUT', 60);        // int; non-numeric values fall back to the default
$debug   = Env::bool('APP_DEBUG', false);         // bool
$raw     = Env::get('SOME_KEY');                  // ?string, null when unset
```

`Env::bool()` treats `true`, `1`, `yes` and `on` as true, and `false`, `0`, `no` and `off` as false (case-insensitive). Any other value returns the default.
`'mail.host'` reads `$config['mail']['host']`, and you can go as deep as your config array does. An exact top-level key is tried first, so a key that literally contains a dot still works.

Method | Accepts | Missing key
`string($key, $default = null)` | Strings, ints and floats | Throws, unless you pass a default
`int($key, $default = null)` | Ints and whole-number strings such as `'587'` | Throws, unless you pass a default
`bool($key, $default = null)` | Bools, and the values `true`, `false`, `1`, `0`, `on`, `off`, `yes`, `no` | Throws, unless you pass a default
`array($key, $default = null)` | Arrays | Throws, unless you pass a default
`get($key, $default = null)` | Anything (no type check) | Returns the default
`has($key)` | Returns `true` if the key exists, even when its value is `null` | Returns `false`
`all()` | Returns the whole config array | –

Because config values often come from `.env` (where everything is a string), the scalar getters are forgiving about format: `'587'` reads as the integer `587`, and `'true'` or `'on'` reads as `true`. A value of `null` counts as missing for the typed getters, so the default applies, or they throw if you gave none.

The exception messages name the key, so a misconfiguration is easy to track down:

```text
Missing config key 'mail.host'.
Config key 'mail.port' must be int, string given.
```

- `Config` throws on a missing or wrongly-typed key, because a broken setting is a bug in your application.
- `Env` falls back to the default you supply, so an unset variable is never fatal.
- `Request` accessors ( `string()`, `int()`, `bool()`, `array()`) also fall back to a default, because user input is expected to be messy. See The Request Object.

In tests you can build a reader directly from an array: `new Config(['mail' => ['host' => 'smtp.test']])`. More on these helpers is on the Support Helpers page.
Rhapsody uses Twig for templating. The framework looks for view files in a specific order, making it easy to override core templates or build custom themes.

The default view directories are:

```bash
views/
├── themes/
│   ├── default/                ← Fallback theme (always available)
│   │   
│   └── my_custom_theme/        ← Your active theme (if set)
│       ├── layouts/
│       └── home/
└── vendor/arout/rhapsody-core/resources/views/themes/       ← Core framework views (default, but overridable.)
    ├── default/
    ├── docs/
    └── ...
```

When you render a view from your controller (e.g., `$this->view('home/index.twig')`), the framework searches in this order:

1. Active theme – `views/themes//` ← this is what you currently have set in `.env`
2. Default theme – `views/themes/default/`
3. Core views – `/vendor/arout/rhapsody-core/resources/views/themes/default/`

Danger: - Never - modify or add view files in the `/vendor` directory. It is only listed above for informational purposes. Instead, if you want to use the framework's styling/theme, create a new `default` directory in `/views/themes/` if it does not already exist.

If a template exists in your active theme, it is used. Otherwise, the framework falls back to the default theme, and finally to the core view. The application will throw a fatal error if it cannot find your template in one of the above directories.

Define the theme in your `.env` file:

```bash
APP_THEME=my_custom_theme
```

If not set, the default theme is used.

To override a core template (e.g., the main layout), simply create a file with the same path inside your active theme. For example, to override `views/core/layouts/main.twig`, create `views/themes/my_custom_theme/layouts/main.twig`.

You can also extend core templates using Twig’s `{% extends %}` tag with the `@core` namespace:

```twig
{% extends "@core/layouts/main.twig" %}
```

If you need additional view directories (e.g., for reusable modules), you can add them to the Twig loader in `bootstrap.php`:

```php
$loader->addPath(__DIR__ . '/modules/blog/views', 'blog');
```

Then render a view using the namespace: `$this->view('@blog/index.twig')`.
Custom error pages (404, 500, etc.) can be placed in `themes//errors/`. The framework will automatically use the theme’s error template if it exists, falling back to the default theme.
See the Middleware documentation for details on setting up middleware.

Switch between `file` and `redis` drivers in `.env`:

```bash
CACHE_DRIVER=redis
REDIS_HOST=127.0.0.1
REDIS_PORT=6379
```
Configure log paths in `config.php` under the `logging` key.

Rhapsody Framework — CLI Reference • Generated with ❤️

Rhapsody's `Rhapsody\Core\Container` is the framework's dependency injection (DI) container. That's a fancy way of saying: it's the thing that builds your objects for you and hands them their dependencies, so you don't have to wire everything up by hand.

You tell the container two things: what you want (an interface, a class name, or a plain string alias like `'config'`) and how to build it (a concrete class name, or a function that returns the object). Then, whenever you need an object, you ask the container for it. If that object needs other objects to be constructed, the container figures those out too — recursively — by inspecting the class's constructor with PHP's Reflection API. In practice, you rarely have to write `new Something(...)` yourself.

- Binds names to things. An interface or alias can be mapped to a concrete class or to a factory function (a closure).
- Auto-wires constructor dependencies. If a class's constructor asks for `LoggerInterface` and `UserRepository`, the container will resolve both and pass them in — recursively, all the way down.
- Calls methods and closures with injection. `call()` invokes any callable and fills its type-hinted parameters from the container — the same way constructors are filled.
- Detects circular dependencies. If `A` needs `B` and `B` needs `A`, the container stops immediately and tells you, instead of looping forever.
- Supports singletons. `singleton()` bindings are built once and then reused on every later request.
- Traces every resolution. Class name, how long it took, who asked for it — all logged for debugging.

- Parameters are resolved in this order: a value passed by name, then a class or interface type-hint (through `resolve()`, so aliases and singletons apply), then the parameter's default value. If none apply, `call()` throws and names the parameter and the function.
- Only public methods can be called. A protected or private method throws instead of being invoked.
- `call()` is part of `ContainerInterface`, so it is available on whatever `Container::getInstance()` returns.
- Exceptions thrown by the callable are not caught.

Two methods exist for managing already-resolved singletons without triggering a new resolution:

- `resolved(string $abstract): bool` — returns `true` if this singleton has already been built and cached on this container.
- `forgetSingleton(string $abstract): void` — drops the cached instance, so the next `resolve()` call rebuilds it from scratch.

These matter most under a persistent-worker runtime (see RoadRunner Persistent Workers), where the container is built once and reused for the life of the worker. `forgetSingleton()` lets you recover a singleton that entered an unusable state mid-request — for example, an `EntityManager` that Doctrine has permanently closed after an unrecoverable ORM exception — without restarting the whole worker.

Pros: no need to thread the container through classes that only need it occasionally; avoids forcing every constructor along a call chain to accept and forward a dependency it doesn't itself use; works identically under a persistent-worker runtime, since `setInstance()` only ever needs to run once at boot.

Cons: pulling a dependency out of a global hides it from a class's public API — a caller can no longer tell what a class needs just by reading its constructor. It also makes unit testing harder, since a test now has to call `Container::setInstance()` with a suitable double before exercising the class, rather than simply passing one in. Reserve `getInstance()` for classes the container doesn't itself resolve — anything the container builds for you (controllers, services bound via `bind()`/`singleton()`) should keep using constructor injection.

- `bind()` always creates a new instance. If you want something shared, use `singleton()`.
- No contextual binding. You can't say "give this class implementation X of the interface, but give that class implementation Y." One binding per abstract, period.
- `call()` injects by type, not by position. Scalars and untyped parameters can only come from `$parameters` (by name) or a default value. Variadic parameters get no special treatment: a typed one receives a single resolved instance, and a scalar one throws unless you pass a value by name (it is passed as one argument).
- The resolution trace is static and shared. `getTrace()` returns the same log across every container instance in the process.
- A string that is also callable is called, not resolved. A string concrete naming a global function or a static method ( `'Foo::create'`) is invoked as a factory, exactly as before. Any other string is treated as a class name.
- No implicit interface autowiring. An interface must be explicitly `bind()`'d to a concrete class before it can be resolved.

Controllers are the central traffic cops of your application. Their primary responsibility is to handle incoming requests, interact with the necessary models to retrieve data, and then pass that data to the appropriate view to be rendered. This keeps your application logic separate from your presentation logic.

All controllers should be placed in the `app/Controllers` directory and should extend the `Rhapsody\Core\BaseController`.

The `BaseController` provides a rich set of helper methods and automatically injects core services so you can focus on your application logic. When you extend it, your controller automatically gains:

- A configured Twig environment with theme support and custom extensions.
- Access to the database via the `$this->db` property.
- Access to the cache via `$this->cache`.
- Built-in SEO helpers (Schema.org structured data).
- Twig extensions for React islands, named routes, and CSRF protection.

Rhapsody includes a first‑class integration with React via the `react()` method. This mounts a React component as a full‑page HTML response, with props serialised safely and Vite assets injected automatically.

```php
public function dashboard(): Response
{
    return $this->react('Dashboard', [
        'user'  => auth()->user()->toArray(),
        'stats' => $this->getDashboardStats(),
    ], [
        'title' => 'Dashboard',
    ]);
}
```

The `react()` method handles:

- Serialising props as JSON (XSS‑safe).
- Injecting the CSRF token as a `<meta>` tag.
- Resolving Vite assets (development HMR or production manifest).
- Rendering a complete HTML document with the component mounted at `#rhapsody-root`.

For more details, see the React Integration documentation.

The debug toolbar includes a Services panel that shows:

- Which services were resolved during the request.
- How long each service took to instantiate.
- Whether the service was lazy‑loaded (green "Yes") or eager (red "No").

This is invaluable for identifying bottlenecks in your controller's dependency graph.

The Middleware panel shows execution times for all middleware, helping you pinpoint slow components.

- Learn about Routing to map URLs to controllers.
- Explore the Request and Response objects.
- Read about React Integration for building modern SPAs.
- Check the Performance guide for lazy loading and caching.

Rhapsody provides a secure, modern API for managing browser cookies and `localStorage` directly from your PHP controllers and Twig templates. Both systems are designed with security and ease of use in mind, leveraging PHP 8.4 features like enums and typed properties.

The `Rhapsody\Core\Storage\Cookie` class offers a static API to set, get, and delete cookies with secure defaults. All cookie values are encrypted using AES-256-CBC and signed with your application's `APP_KEY`, preventing client-side tampering.

Before using cookies, ensure your `.env` file contains a 32-character encryption key:

```bash
APP_KEY=your-32-character-secret-key
```

Generate one with: `php -r "echo bin2hex(random_bytes(16));"`
The `Rhapsody\Core\Storage\LocalStorage` class generates JavaScript snippets that manipulate the browser's `localStorage`. This is useful for client-side preferences, temporary data, or caching.

- Encryption: All cookies are encrypted with your `APP_KEY`.
- HttpOnly: By default, cookies are not accessible via JavaScript, preventing XSS attacks.
- SameSite: Defaults to `Lax`, protecting against CSRF.
- Secure: By default, cookies are only sent over HTTPS (set `secure=false` only for local development).
- LocalStorage: Data is stored in plain text in the browser – never store sensitive information (like passwords or tokens) in `localStorage`.

In your PHPUnit tests, you can mock the cookie functions or use the `Cookie::get()` and `Cookie::set()` methods as usual. For `localStorage`, the generated JavaScript is not executed in unit tests, so you may want to test the generation logic separately.
Rhapsody provides a lightweight PDO wrapper with support for multiple database drivers and query logging for debugging.

Configure your database connection in the `.env` file:

```bash
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=3306
DB_NAME=your_database
DB_USER=your_username
DB_PASS=your_password
DB_DRIVER="mysql" # mysql, pgsql, sqlite, or sqlsrv
```

- MySQL – Default driver
- PostgreSQL ( `pgsql`)
- SQLite – Use `:memory:` for in-memory testing
- SQL Server ( `sqlsrv`)

The `Database` class is a singleton that lazily connects to the database on first use. This means pages that don't need the database won't open a connection.

Pro tip: It is best practice to place database queries inside models, rather than in your controllers (separation of concerns). This will keep your controllers clutter-free and make testing / maintaining your code much simpler. See models documentation for more information.
The debug toolbar automatically detects and warns about N+1 query patterns when the same query is executed multiple times.

Rhapsody includes a built‑in DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) protection middleware that limits the number of requests a single IP address can make within a given time window. When the limit is exceeded, the middleware returns a `429 Too Many Requests` response with a `Retry‑After` header, preventing abuse.

The protection is implemented as a global middleware (`Rhapsody\Core\Middleware\DdosMiddleware`). It runs on every request and tracks the request count per IP address using the framework’s cache system (file, Redis, etc.).

Once an IP exceeds the configured `max_requests` within the `time_window` (in seconds), it is blocked for the `block_duration` (in seconds). During the block period, all subsequent requests from that IP receive a `429` response.

All settings are defined in your `config.php` file under the DDoS keys. You can also override them via environment variables in your `.env` file.

Config Key | Environment Variable | Default | Description
`ddos_max_requests` | `DDOS_MAX_REQUESTS` | 60 | Maximum allowed requests within the time window.
`ddos_time_window` | `DDOS_TIME_WINDOW` | 60 | Time window in seconds.
`ddos_block_duration` | `DDOS_BLOCK_DURATION` | 300 | How long (in seconds) to block the IP after the limit is exceeded.
`ddos_whitelist` | `DDOS_WHITELIST` | `127.0.0.100,::100` | Comma‑separated list of IP addresses that are never blocked (useful for internal services).
`ddos_blacklist` | `DDOS_BLACKLIST` | — | Comma‑separated list of IPs that are immediately blocked.

```
DDOS_MAX_REQUESTS=10
DDOS_TIME_WINDOW=30
DDOS_BLOCK_DURATION=120
DDOS_WHITELIST=127.0.0.1,::1,192.168.1.100
```
The middleware is automatically enabled when you include it in the `middleware.global` array in `config.php`. To disable it, simply remove it from that list.

The default response is a user‑friendly HTML page. If you need to return JSON (for API endpoints), you can override the `rateLimitExceededResponse()` method in your own middleware or extend the core class.

The rate limiter uses the framework’s cache driver (`file`, `redis`, or `memcached`). For production, it is recommended to use a shared cache like Redis when running multiple servers behind a load balancer, so the request counters are synchronised.

You can simulate heavy traffic using tools like `ab` (Apache Bench) or a simple loop with `curl`:

```bash
for i in {1..20}; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "Request $i: %{http_code}\n" http://your-site.com/; done
```

After exceeding the limit, you should see `429` status codes.

The DDoS protection is part of the core middleware system. For more advanced use cases (e.g., endpoint‑specific limits, CAPTCHA challenges), you can extend the provided classes or write your own middleware.

Rhapsody includes a set of global helper functions to simplify debugging and inspecting variables during development. These helpers are available everywhere – in controllers, models, commands, and even in your view files (though not recommended).

If Symfony VarDumper is installed (it comes with `filp/whoops`), this provides the same pretty output as `dd()` but without terminating the script. It’s an alias for `Symfony\Component\VarDumper\VarDumper::dump()`.

The helpers are defined in `core/helpers.php`, which is automatically loaded via Composer. They use the Symfony VarDumper component (already a dependency of Whoops) for advanced formatting – including syntax highlighting, expandable arrays/objects, and proper recursion handling.

If VarDumper is not available, the helpers fall back to simple `var_dump()`.

- Never commit `dd()` or `d()` to production code. They are strictly for local development.
- Use `dd($user)` instead of multiple `var_dump()` calls – it’s cleaner and safer.
- You can pass any number of arguments: `dd($user, $posts, $_SERVER);`
- In Twig templates, you can use `{{ dump(user) }}` if you add the Twig extension, but it’s not enabled by default. For quick debugging in views, consider dumping from the controller instead.

Security Note: In production, `APP_ENV=production`, the `dump()` function still works but may expose sensitive data. Remove all debugging calls before deploying.

Method | What it does
`defer(callable $task)` | Queues a task. It is called with no arguments, so capture what it needs with `use (...)`.
`pending()` | How many tasks are waiting to run.
`discard()` | Drops every waiting task without running it.
`flush()` | Finishes the response and runs the waiting tasks. The framework calls this for you; you should not need to.

The framework detects the environment and picks the best behaviour automatically.

Environment | What happens
PHP-FPM or LiteSpeed | The response is flushed and the connection is closed, then tasks run. The visitor never waits.
Apache `mod_php`, the built-in server | The response is fully flushed, then tasks run. The page is complete in the browser, but the connection stays open until the tasks finish.
RoadRunner worker | Tasks run right after the response is handed to RoadRunner. That worker is busy until they finish.
`php rhapsody` commands and other CLI scripts | There is no response to wait for, so the task runs immediately when you call `defer()`.

- Tasks cannot change the response. By the time they run, the headers and body are gone. Anything a task prints is discarded.
- The session is already closed. The session lock is released before tasks run so the visitor's next request is not blocked. Writing to the session inside a task will not persist.
- Failures are logged, never shown. A task that throws is written to `storage/logs/defer.log` and the remaining tasks still run.
- A failed request runs nothing. If the request ends in an exception (including a 404 or 500 page), its queued tasks are discarded.
- Tasks run in the order you queued them, and a task may call `defer()` to queue more. A single request runs at most 1000 tasks.
- PHP time limits still apply. Under PHP-FPM, `max_execution_time` and `request_terminate_timeout` apply to deferred work too. Closing the connection does not remove them.
- Nothing is saved. If the server stops while a task is waiting, the task is lost. For work that must survive that (payments, important emails), use a persistent queue instead.
- Resolve it by its interface. Ask the container for `DeferrerInterface::class`, not the concrete class.
- Boot-time code: the `defer()` helper is available once the application has finished booting. A module's `boot()` runs earlier, so resolve `DeferrerInterface` from the container there instead.

Tip: keep deferred tasks small and self-contained. Capture plain values (an id, an email address) rather than whole request objects, so the task does not depend on request state that no longer matters.

- Sessions
- Logging
- The Service Container

For developers who prefer a powerful Object-Relational Mapper (ORM), Rhapsody comes fully integrated with Doctrine. This allows you to work with your database using objects and entities, abstracting away raw SQL for more complex applications. This feature is available alongside the original PDO-based BaseModel, giving you the freedom to choose the right tool for your needs.

In Doctrine, an "Entity" is a PHP class that maps directly to a database table. Each property in the class corresponds to a column in that table. All entity files should be placed in the `app/Entities/` directory.

You define the mapping using PHP Attributes, which makes the configuration clean and readable.
Once the `EntityManager` is available in your controller (e.g., as `$this->em`), you can perform database operations.

Rhapsody ships with a small, fast encryption service built on PHP's bundled OpenSSL extension. It covers the four things most applications actually need: encrypting a value, signing a value so tampering is detectable, signed URLs, and encrypted database columns. There are no extra Composer dependencies, and the service is only instantiated if your code uses it.

Encryption is authenticated (AES-256-GCM): a payload that was modified, or that was produced with a different key, simply fails to decrypt. The framework's own cookie storage is built on this service.

Everything is derived from the `APP_KEY` in your `.env` file. The key must be at least 32 bytes; 64 random hex characters is recommended:

```bash
APP_KEY=your-64-character-hex-key
```

Generate one with: `php -r "echo bin2hex(random_bytes(32));"`

Separate encryption and signing keys are derived from `APP_KEY` using HKDF, so you only ever manage one secret. If `APP_KEY` is missing or too short, the first use of the service throws an exception rather than falling back to an insecure default.

Every method accepts an optional context string that is cryptographically bound to the result. A value encrypted under one context will not decrypt under another, which prevents a valid payload from being copied somewhere it was never meant to go.

```php
$token = $encrypter->encrypt('42', 'invoice-download');

$encrypter->decrypt($token, 'invoice-download'); // "42"
$encrypter->decrypt($token, 'password-reset');   // null
$encrypter->decrypt($token);                     // null
```

Changing `APP_KEY` would normally make everything encrypted with the old key unreadable. To rotate without breaking existing data, move the old key into `APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS` (comma-separated):

```bash
APP_KEY=the-new-64-character-hex-key
APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS=the-old-key,an-even-older-key
```

New data is always written with `APP_KEY`. When reading, the current key is tried first, then each previous key. Once you are confident nothing encrypted with an old key remains (cookies have expired, database columns have been re-saved), remove it from the list.

Method | Description
`encrypt(string $plaintext, string $context = '')` | Encrypts and authenticates a string. Returns a URL and cookie-safe string.
`decrypt(string $payload, string $context = '')` | Returns the original string, or `null` if the payload is invalid, altered, or bound to another context.
`sign(string $value, string $context = '')` | Returns `value.signature`. The value remains readable.
`unsign(string $signed, string $context = '')` | Returns the original value, or `null` if the signature doesn't match.
`signature(string $data, string $context = '')` | Returns a detached, URL-safe signature for any data.
`verifySignature(string $data, string $signature, string $context = '')` | Timing-safe check of a detached signature.
`UrlSigner::sign(string $url, ?int $ttlSeconds = null)` | Returns the URL with a signature (and optional expiry) appended.
`UrlSigner::verify(string $url)` | Returns `true` if the signature is valid and the link has not expired.

- Passwords: never encrypt passwords. Hash them with `password_hash()` and verify with `password_verify()`.
- CSRF tokens and sessions: these are random values stored server-side and compared directly. Encrypting them adds cost without adding security.
- Secrets the browser must read: encryption protects data from the client, but the server holds the key. Data that JavaScript needs (for example in `localStorage`) cannot be protected this way.

The encrypted payload format changed when this service was introduced (a version byte and a per-cookie context were added). Cookies set by earlier versions of Rhapsody will no longer decrypt: `Cookie::get()` returns your default value for them, exactly as it does for a tampered cookie, and the next `Cookie::set()` replaces them. PHP sessions are not affected.

`Cookie::setEncryptionKey()` has been removed. The key now always comes from `APP_KEY` (and `APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS`). If your own code called it, delete the call.

Rhapsody includes a robust global error handler that catches exceptions, converts PHP errors to exceptions, and handles fatal shutdown errors. In development you get detailed Whoops pages; in production you get clean, user‑friendly error pages while all errors are logged.

The `Rhapsody\Core\ErrorHandler` class is registered early in `index.php`. It sets three PHP handlers:

- `set_error_handler()` – converts warnings, notices, etc. into `ErrorException`.
- `set_exception_handler()` – catches all uncaught exceptions.
- `register_shutdown_function()` – catches fatal errors (e.g., missing class, parse errors).

The error handler reads the `logging` array from `config.php`. Add the `error_log_path` to specify where errors should be written:

```php
'logging' => [
    'error_log_path' => __DIR__ . '/storage/logs/errors.log',
    // other log paths...
],
```

When an error occurs, the handler displays a Whoops error page with:

- Full stack trace with clickable file links.
- Code snippet around the error line.
- Environment and request data.
- Interactive console to inspect variables.

Errors are still logged, but the visual feedback helps you debug quickly.

When an AI client is configured, the development error page also shows an Explain and fix with AI button. It opens a side panel that asks the model why the request failed and, when the cause is in your own code, proposes a change.

- Nothing is sent until you have reviewed the exact text, which includes the exception, a redacted picture of the request and a few lines of source code around the failing lines. Secrets are masked first.
- A proposed fix is shown as a diff. It is only written to disk when you click Apply this change twice, and the original file is saved first.
- Code in `vendor/`, `config/` and `.env` files is never edited.

See AI Assistant for what is sent and the `debug.assist` options. In production the button and its URLs do not exist.

The handler shows a generic error page to the user – no sensitive details are leaked. Meanwhile, the full error (including stack trace) is written to the configured log file.

By default, HTTP status codes are respected:

- 404 Not Found – when a route doesn’t match.
- 500 Internal Server Error – for all other exceptions.

You can create custom Twig templates for error pages. Place them in `views/errors/` with the status code as the filename: - `views/errors/404.twig` – shown when a page is not found. - `views/errors/500.twig` – shown for server errors. - You can add any HTTP status code (e.g., `403.twig`, `503.twig`). Example `404.twig`: ```twig {% extends "layouts/main.twig" %} {% block title %}404 Not Found{% endblock %} {% block content %}

404

Page not found.

Go Home
{% endblock %} ``` If no custom view exists for a status code, the handler falls back to a simple HTML error message.

Each error is logged using the `Rhapsody\Core\Logger` class. A typical log entry looks like:

```php
[2025-06-15 14:32:10] ERROR: [PDOException] SQLSTATE[42S02]: Base table or view not found in /var/www/app/Models/User.php:45
Stack trace:
#0 /var/www/app/Models/User.php(45): PDO->prepare()
#1 /var/www/app/Controllers/UserController.php(22): App\Models\User->findById()
#2 /var/www/core/Router.php(89): App\Controllers\UserController->show()
...
```
In rare cases (e.g., running unit tests), you may want to disable the custom handler. Call `restore_error_handler()` and `restore_exception_handler()` manually.

Rhapsody includes a simple but powerful event dispatcher system that allows you to decouple various aspects of your application. By dispatching events, you can allow other parts of your application, or "listeners," to react to an action without the original code needing to know about them. This is a great way to handle side effects, like sending a notification email after a user registers.

This approach follows the Observer design pattern and leads to a more modular and maintainable codebase.

1. An action occurs in your application (e.g., a user registers).
2. Your controller creates and dispatches an `Event` object containing data about what happened.
3. The `EventDispatcher` receives the event and finds all registered Listeners for it.
4. The dispatcher runs each listener in the order it was registered, passing it the event object: the `handle()` method of a listener class, or a callable directly.
The Rhapsody console includes generator commands to quickly create new event and listener classes for your application.

This command will create a new event class in the `app/Events` directory. Events are simple data objects that hold information about the event.

```bash
php rhapsody make:event UserRegistered
```

You can then edit the generated `UserRegistered.php` file to accept data in its constructor, like the user object.

This command creates a new listener class in the `app/Listeners` directory. Listeners contain the logic to handle an event.

```bash
php rhapsody make:listener SendWelcomeEmail
```

You will then implement the logic for sending the email inside the `handle()` method of the generated `SendWelcomeEmail.php` file.

headingPath: 4. Listener Types and Registering at Runtime
chunks.text:
A listener can be either of two things:

Listener | How it runs
A class name, e.g. `SendWelcomeEmail::class` | The class is created by the service container, so its constructor dependencies (a mailer, the entity manager...) are injected automatically. Its `handle($event)` method is then called. A class with no `handle()` method but an `__invoke()` method is invoked instead.
A callable: a closure, or an `[$object, 'method']` pair | Called directly with the event.

A plain string is always treated as a class name. To run a function by name, wrap it in a closure.

headingPath: 4. Listener Types and Registering at Runtime
4. Listener Types and Registering at Runtime
chunks.text:
In the `EventServiceProvider` you can give an event either a single listener or a list. Several listeners run in the order they are listed.

```php
protected array $listen = [
    UserRegistered::class => SendWelcomeEmail::class,                       // one listener
    OrderPlaced::class    => [NotifyWarehouse::class, EmailReceipt::class], // several, in order
];
```

headingPath: 4. Listener Types and Registering at Runtime
4. Listener Types and Registering at Runtime
chunks.text: `Rhapsody\Core\Contracts\ListenerInterface` describes a listener whose `handle(Event $event)` accepts any event. The dispatcher does not require it: it only needs a `handle()` method (or a callable). A listener that handles one specific event, like `handle(UserRegistered $event)`, simply declares that method and does not implement the interface.

headingPath: 4. Listener Types and Registering at Runtime
chunks.text: Listeners are looked up by the exact class of the dispatched event. A listener registered for a parent class or an interface does not run for its subclasses, and there are no wildcards. Register the listener for each concrete event class you want it to hear.

- Order: listeners for an event run in the order they were registered. Their return values are ignored.
- A failing listener does not break the request. If a listener throws (a mail server is down, say), the dispatcher catches the exception, writes a line to the PHP error log naming the listener and the event, and carries on with the next listener. The code that called `dispatch()` never sees the exception.
- Nested events are capped. A listener may dispatch further events, but nesting more than 8 levels deep is skipped and logged. This is only a backstop against listeners that trigger each other in a loop; real chains are one or two levels deep.
- `dispatch()` returns the event. You usually ignore it, but for a stoppable event it is how you read the answer a listener supplied.

Don't put must-succeed work in a listener. Because a failing listener is logged and skipped, anything that has to happen (charging a card, saving the order) belongs in your controller or service, not in an event listener. Use listeners for side effects such as emails, notifications and statistics.

headingPath: 6. Event Classes Included with the Framework
chunks.text:
Class (`Rhapsody\Core\Events`) | Public properties
`UserRegistered` | `$user`
`PaymentSucceededEvent` | `$transactionId`, `$amount`, `$metadata` (array)
`PaymentFailedEvent` | `$message`, `$context` (array)
`RouteNotFound` | `$uri`, `$method`, plus `setResponse()` / `getResponse()` (a stoppable event)

Everything above describes the normal way events work in Rhapsody: dispatching an event is fire-and-forget. The code that calls `dispatch()` doesn't wait to see what listeners do, and nothing a listener does can change what happens next. This is true for `UserRegistered`, and it's true for almost every event you'll ever write — the whole point of events is to let listeners react to something without the original code needing to know or care.

A very small number of events in the framework break that rule on purpose: they let a listener supply an answer that the dispatching code actually uses. The framework ships one example of this, `Rhapsody\Core\Events\RouteNotFound`, which the router dispatches right before it gives up and shows a 404 page — see the Routing documentation for that specific example. This section explains the general mechanism behind it, in case you ever need to build something similar for your own application.

chunks.text: Rhapsody includes a small, secure file uploader: a fluent PHP class that validates and stores files, and a drop-in JavaScript file that adds per-file progress bars to any upload form.

- `images()` – JPEG, PNG, GIF and WebP. (SVG is excluded because it can contain scripts.)
- `documents()` – PDF, plain text and Word documents.
- `accept('application/zip', 'image/*')` – any MIME types; wildcards like `image/*` are supported. Calls accumulate, so `images()->accept('application/pdf')` allows both.
- `acceptAny()` – explicitly allow every type. Executable extensions such as `.php` are still never preserved.
- `maxSize('5MB')` – per-file limit. Accepts bytes ( `5242880`) or strings like `'512KB'`, `'5MB'`, `'1GB'`. Defaults to 5 MB.
- `to('/absolute/path')` – store somewhere other than `storage/uploads`.

Allowed types are required. Calling `store()` without `images()`, `documents()`, `accept()` or `acceptAny()` throws a `LogicException`, so you can never accidentally accept everything.

Note: your PHP limits (`upload_max_filesize` and `post_max_size` in `php.ini`) apply before Rhapsody sees the file. When a request exceeds `post_max_size` the uploader reports it clearly.

Include `public/js/rhapsody-uploader.js` and add `data-rhapsody-upload` (the endpoint URL) to any form that contains a file input. Put `csrf_field()` inside the form; the script sends the `_token` value with every file. ```html
{{ csrf_field() }}
    ``` The `
      ` is optional; it is created automatically if you leave it out. A complete, styled example lives in `views/upload.twig`.

- The script intercepts `submit` and sends each file in its own `XMLHttpRequest`. XHR is used because, unlike `fetch()`, it reports upload progress. A separate request per file also means each file gets its own progress bar and error message.
- The submit button is disabled while uploads are running, and the progress list is announced to screen readers ( `aria-live`).
- Server errors are read from the JSON response ( `errors[filename]`), so the messages from `UploadResult` appear next to the right file.

The script injects no CSS and uses the native `<progress>` element. Style it with attribute selectors: `li[data-state="waiting|uploading|success|error"]`, `[data-role="name"]`, `progress` and `[data-role="status"]`.

- The MIME type is detected from the file's contents ( `finfo`), not from the browser-supplied type.
- Stored filenames are random and extensions come from the detected type, so an uploaded `shell.php` can never be saved as executable code.
- Uploads go to `storage/uploads`, outside the web root. Serve them through a controller rather than linking to them directly.
- Keep the upload route behind CSRF protection. The JavaScript sends the token for you.

Rhapsody uses League Glide, an on-demand image manipulation library built on Intervention Image, to resize, crop, convert, and compress images simply by changing the URL. Every variant is generated once, cached on disk, and served from the cache afterwards, saving storage space and improving performance.

First, add the library to your project using Composer:

```bash
composer require league/glide
```

Glide needs either the `gd` or the `imagick` PHP extension. GD is enabled by default in most PHP installations, including WAMP.

An `ImageController` is included in the application skeleton to handle all image requests. For each request it validates the URL signature, asks Glide for the matching image variant (generating and caching it the first time), and returns it with the correct `Content-Type` and caching headers.

By default, source images are read from the `public/images/` directory (see Changing the Image Directory to use another one), and processed images are stored in `storage/cache/images/`. Ensure the cache directory is writable by your web server. Image paths are always relative to the source directory, so the file `public/images/wrestlers/hogan.webp` is requested as `wrestlers/hogan.webp`.

- Image paths are relative to the new directory. With the example above, the file `public/themes/default/images/logo.png` is requested as `image_url('logo.png', {w: 200})`.
- Serving several themes. Glide reads from one directory at a time. Point `source` at the parent folder, `Path::public('themes')`, and include the theme in the image path ( `image_url('default/images/logo.png', {w: 200})`) to reach every theme from a single setting.
- Choosing the theme at runtime. If you build the directory from a variable, such as `Path::public('themes/' . $theme . '/images')`, take `$theme` from your application's configuration, never from the request. A value supplied by a visitor could point the processor at an arbitrary directory.
- Originals do not have to be public. Every image is served through the controller, so the source directory can live outside `public/`, for example `Path::storage('uploads/images')`.
- Clear the image cache after changing the directory. Cached variants are stored in folders named after the image path, so a file with the same name in the old and new directories can be served from the old cache. Delete the contents of `storage/cache/images/` once.

Use the `image_url()` Twig function to build the image source. It takes the image path (relative to `public/images/`) and an optional object of parameters, and returns a complete, signed URL. **Example: Resizing an Image** Let's say you have an image located at `public/images/wrestlers/hogan.webp`. Original HTML: ```html ``` Optimized HTML with resizing: ```html ``` **Example: Responsive Images** Generate each size you need in the template and let the browser choose: ```html ```

Every distinct set of query parameters creates a separate cached file, so unrestricted resizing would let anyone fill your disk and CPU by requesting thousands of sizes. To prevent this, image variants must be signed by your application:

- A request with query parameters must carry a valid `s` signature. Missing, invalid, or edited signatures return 403.
- A request without query parameters (the plain original image, e.g. `/img/wrestlers/hogan.webp`) is public and needs no signature.
- The signature covers the image path and every parameter, so changing `w=300` to `w=3000` in a signed URL invalidates it.

Always build URLs with `image_url()` in Twig. Outside of templates, use the same signer in PHP:

```php
use Rhapsody\Core\Helpers\ImageSigner;

$url = ImageSigner::url('wrestlers/hogan.webp', ['w' => 300, 'q' => 80]);
```

URLs assembled in JavaScript cannot be signed, because the signing key must stay on the server. Generate each size you need in Twig (for example in a `srcset`) instead of building query strings in the browser.

**Signing Key**

Signatures are made with the `IMAGE_SIGN_KEY` value from your `.env` file when it is set. Otherwise a separate key is derived from your `APP_KEY` (the raw `APP_KEY` is never used directly). If neither is set, generating a URL throws an exception.

```bash
# .env (optional)
IMAGE_SIGN_KEY=a-long-random-string
```

Changing the key invalidates every previously signed URL, including URLs saved in cached pages. Set `IMAGE_SIGN_KEY` if you want to rotate the image key independently of `APP_KEY`.

Pass these as the second argument of `image_url()`. Glide supports many more, documented in the Glide documentation.

Parameter | Description
`w` | The target width in pixels.
`h` | The target height in pixels. If only one dimension is provided, the image is scaled proportionally.
`fit` | How the image is fitted to `w` and `h`: `contain` (default) fits inside the box keeping the aspect ratio; `max` does the same but never enlarges a smaller image; `fill` fits inside the box and fills the leftover space with the `bg` color; `stretch` ignores the aspect ratio; `crop` fills the box exactly, cropping the overflow (also `crop-top-left`, `crop-bottom-right` and the other position variants).
`q` | The compression quality from 0 to 100 for JPEG and WebP output. Defaults to 90.
`fm` | The output format: `jpg`, `pjpg` (progressive JPEG), `png`, `gif`, or `webp`. Defaults to the source format.
`dpr` | Device pixel ratio from 1 to 8. Multiplies `w` and `h` for high-density screens.
`bg` | Background color (hex or named), used by `fit: 'fill'` and when converting transparent images to JPEG.
`or` | Orientation: `auto`, `0`, `90`, `180`, or `270`.
`blur`, `sharp`, `filt` | Blur (0–100), sharpen (0–100), and filters (`greyscale`, `sepia`).

The first request for a variant generates it and stores it under `storage/cache/images/`, in a folder named after the source image, with one file per unique parameter combination. Later requests are served from that file. Responses are sent with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400`, so browsers and CDNs keep them for a day.

If you replace a source image, delete its folder inside `storage/cache/images/` (or the whole directory) so variants are regenerated from the new file.

The largest image Glide will generate is 4,000,000 pixels (width × height, equal to 2000×2000). Larger sources and requests are scaled down to fit, even when no size is requested. To change the limit, edit the `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` constant in `ImageController`.

- 403 Invalid image signature — the URL was built by hand, edited, or built in JavaScript. Generate it with `image_url()`.
- 404 Image not found — the path is relative to the image source directory ( `public/images/` by default). Use `wrestlers/hogan.webp`, not `public/images/wrestlers/hogan.webp`.
- An exception about `APP_KEY` or `IMAGE_SIGN_KEY` — set one of them in your `.env` file.
- Cache errors — make sure `storage/cache/images/` exists and is writable by your web server.

Rhapsody is a lightweight, modern PHP framework designed for building elegant and maintainable web applications. It follows a familiar MVC-like architecture and provides a solid foundation with powerful features like a flexible router, a secure authentication system, a robust validation engine, and an efficient templating system powered by Twig.

This documentation will guide you through the installation, configuration, and core concepts of the framework. Use the navigation on the left to explore the different components and learn how to build your first application with Rhapsody.

The goal of Rhapsody is to provide a simple yet powerful starting point. It handles the boilerplate and provides essential tools without imposing a rigid structure, giving you the freedom to build your application your way. We believe in clean code, modern PHP features, and a great developer experience.
Getting started with Rhapsody is designed to be a quick and straightforward process. Follow these steps to get your local development environment up and running.

Rhapsody is built with modern PHP. Please ensure your environment meets the following requirements:

- PHP 8.4.1 or higher
- Composer installed
- A local server environment like MAMP, WAMP, or Laravel Herd
- mod_rewrite must be enabled on Apache servers
- PHP's GD extension should be enabled if you plan on using the image resizing/caching helper
- A MySQL-compatible database

Rhapsody is available as a Composer package. To create a new project, run:

```bash
composer create-project arout/rhapsody-app your-site-name
```

This command downloads the framework, installs all PHP dependencies, and sets up the basic structure.

Navigate into your new project directory:

```bash
cd your-site-name
```

It's a good practice to run a Composer update to ensure all dependencies are up‑to‑date and all new features are included:

```bash
composer update
```

⚠️ Important: Before any page will load, you must set at least the following variables in your `.env`:

- `APP_URL` – the full base URL of your site (e.g., `https://your-website.com`)
- `DB_HOST`, `DB_PORT`, `DB_NAME`, `DB_USER`, `DB_PASS`, `DB_DRIVER` – your database connection details

If you plan to use React for SPA's or React Islands (or want the debug toolbar’s Performance and Memory Usage panels to work), you need to set up the React bridge:

```bash
php rhapsody react:install
```

This command installs the necessary npm dependencies and creates the basic React entry point.

After running it, install the JavaScript dependencies and start the Vite development server:

```bash
npm install
npm run dev
```

Note: Even if you don’t use React anywhere else, the debug toolbar’s performance tabs rely on React islands. We recommend running this step to get the full debugging experience.

Rhapsody uses a `.env` file to manage environment‑specific variables. This file is required for the application to run. It is located in your root install directory and should be created automatically during the Composer install process. If for some reason it does not exist, simply run the command below.

Copy the example file:

```bash
cp .env.example .env
```

Example configuration:

```bash
APP_URL="https://your-website.com"
APP_BASE_URL="/{subirectory name}" # Leave blank unless installed in a subdirectory

DB_HOST="127.0.0.1"
DB_PORT="3306"
DB_NAME="database_name"
DB_USER="username"
DB_PASS="password"
DB_DRIVER="mysql" # Supported databases: mysql, pgsql, sqlite, or sqlsrv
```

Without these values, the application will not be able to connect to the database or generate correct URLs.
Create a database with the name you specified in `DB_NAME`. If you want to receive email notifications about updates, set `MAIL_ADMIN_EMAIL` in the .env as well.

Your web server must be configured to direct all requests to the front controller (`index.php`). The repository includes a `.htaccess` file for Apache; for other servers (Nginx, etc.) please consult your server’s documentation.

Once everything is set up, visit your site in the browser – you should see the Rhapsody welcome page.

After installation is complete, you may find it beneficial to run a few commands using the Rhapsody runner (see Rhapsody Console and console commands for a complete command list and using the CLI runner).

Some of the commands you may wish to run immediately after installation:

php rhapsody auth:install | Install authentication tables (users, password_resets, etc.). Run this if you plan on using the built-in authentication system. See authentication for more details.
php rhapsody build:proxies | Pre-generates lazy proxy classes for all container services. See lazy loading for more details.
php rhapsody app:cache-warm | Warm up the Twig template cache by compiling all templates. Recommended for live site only; keep cache disabled in dev environment.
php rhapsody route:cache | Compile all application routes into a cached file for performance. Recommended for live site only; keep cache disabled in dev environment.
The `Kernel` is the core of Rhapsody's request handling. It orchestrates the entire request lifecycle from receiving a `Request` to returning a `Response`.

- Handling – Routes the request and executes middleware.
- Termination – Performs post-response tasks like injecting the debug toolbar.

`Kernel::handle()` is a pure function: Request in, Response out. It delegates to `Router::dispatch()` and normalizes 404/500 status codes into `HttpException` for consistent error handling.

```php
$response = $kernel->handle($request);
```

`Kernel::terminate()` performs post-response tasks that don't affect the meaning of the response:

- Injects the development debug toolbar.
- Adds framework update notifications.

This method is safe to skip entirely (e.g., in production, or for non-HTML responses).
`HttpException` is intentionally allowed to propagate out of `handle()` uncaught. The global `ErrorHandler` (registered in `index.php`) owns turning it into a rendered error page.

1. Environment loaded ( `.env`)
2. Error handler registered
3. Session started
4. Container built
5. Routes loaded
6. Kernel::handle() – middleware & controller executed
7. Kernel::terminate() – debug toolbar & banners injected
8. Response sent to client

Rhapsody includes a powerful lazy‑loading system for the service container. Instead of instantiating every service eagerly at the start of a request, the framework can defer the creation of services until they are actually used. This improves performance, especially in applications with many dependencies or heavy services that are not always needed.

The lazy‑loading system is implemented via a proxy pattern. When you request a service from the container, the `ContainerDecorator` may return a proxy object instead of the real service. The proxy has the same interface as the target class, but it does not instantiate the real object until one of its methods is called.

**Lazy Loading Flow**

1. Your code requests a service via `$container->get(SomeService::class)`
2. The `ContainerDecorator` checks if lazy loading is enabled and if the service is not marked as "eager"
3. A dynamic proxy class is generated (if not already cached) by `ProxyGenerator`
4. The proxy is instantiated with an initializer closure that knows how to resolve the real service
5. The proxy is returned to your code – the real service is not created yet
6. When you call a method on the proxy, the proxy triggers the initializer, instantiates the real service, and forwards the call

This means that heavy services (e.g., those that connect to external APIs, load large datasets, or have complex constructors) will only be built if they are actually used during the request.
Lazy loading is controlled via the `config.php` file under the `lazy` key, or via environment variables.

Some services should never be lazy-loaded – for example, those that must be fully initialised early, or that have side effects in their constructor. You can list them in the `eager` array:

```php
'lazy' => [
    'enabled' => true,
    'eager' => [
        \App\Services\PaymentGateway::class,
        \App\Services\EmailDispatcher::class,
    ],
]
```

Controllers are always resolved eagerly because they are typically needed immediately and their constructors should not be deferred.

- Faster request startup – fewer services are instantiated upfront.
- Lower memory usage – unused services are never created.
- Selective heavy lifting – expensive operations happen only when needed.

- Final classes – cannot be proxied because proxy classes extend the target; `ProxyGenerator` throws an exception if the class is final.
- Constructors are not lazy – the real object is only created when a method is called; constructor logic is deferred until that point.
- Private methods – are not proxied, but that's fine because proxy only forwards public/protected calls.
- Static methods – are not supported for lazy loading (they would bypass the proxy).

- Services that must be fully initialised early for correct operation (e.g., database connection, session handler).
- Services with side effects in their constructor that must happen immediately.
- Services that are used in almost every request (e.g., logging, configuration).

Proxies are generated on‑the‑fly by `ProxyGenerator` and cached in `storage/cache/proxies/`. You can pre‑build proxies for all services using the CLI command:

```bash
php rhapsody build:proxies
```

This can be useful in production to avoid the overhead of generating proxies on the first request.

Service container lazy loading is a powerful optimisation technique that can significantly improve performance by deferring the creation of heavy services until they are actually needed. Combined with the caching system, it provides a robust toolkit for building high‑performance applications.

Note: Lazy loading is enabled by default. You can disable it globally via `LAZY_LOADING_ENABLED=false` in your `.env` file.

Rhapsody includes a simple but effective file-based logger, managed by the `Rhapsody\Core\Logger` class. It provides a standardized way to write messages to log files for debugging, tracking errors, or recording important events in your application.
To use the logger, you create a new instance of the `Rhapsody\Core\Logger` class, passing the path to the desired log file in its constructor.

For uncaught exceptions, PHP errors, and fatal shutdown errors, Rhapsody uses a global error handler that logs everything to a dedicated error log file. See the Error Handling & Logging documentation for details.

All mailer configuration is handled in your `.env` file. You can configure your SMTP host, port, username, and password. For local development, a service like Mailtrap is highly recommended to safely test your emails in a "fake" inbox.

Middleware filters HTTP requests before they reach your controller. Rhapsody includes `auth` and `guest` middleware out of the box, and you can create your own.

Middleware classes must implement a `handle(Request $request): ?Response` method. If the middleware returns a `Response` object (e.g., a redirect or error response), the request is short‑circuited and that response is sent immediately. If it returns `null`, the request proceeds to the next middleware or controller.
Middleware configuration is stored in `config/middleware.php` – never modify files inside `/core`. This keeps your customisations safe during framework updates.

- `auth` – redirects to `/login` if no user is logged in.
- `guest` – redirects to `/dashboard` if a user is already logged in.
- `VerifyCsrfTokenMiddleware` – global middleware that validates CSRF tokens on unsafe methods.

The Model layer is responsible for all interaction with your database. It abstracts the data source so that your controllers don't need to know the specifics of your database schema or write raw SQL queries. In Rhapsody, all models are placed in the `app/Models` directory and should extend the `Rhapsody\Core\BaseModel`.

The framework uses PDO (PHP Data Objects) for database communication, which provides a secure and consistent interface. The database connection is managed by the `Rhapsody\Core\Database` class, which uses a Singleton pattern. This means the application only ever makes one single database connection per request, which is very efficient.

By extending `BaseModel`, your model automatically gets access to the database connection via `$this->db`.

A module can add whole pages to a site: an admin dashboard, a settings screen, a list of records. The problem is that a module author has no idea which theme the site owner will use. If the module writes plain HTML, it looks unstyled next to a fully designed navbar and footer. If it ships its own big stylesheet, it looks foreign on every theme, and every module ends up reinventing forms and tables.

Module UI solves this. It is a small set of ready-made CSS classes (all starting with `rhapsody-`) and a base layout that every module page can build on. The classes look decent on any theme, light or dark, and a theme can fine-tune them if it wants to. This page explains how to use them from scratch.

Who is this page for? Module authors (how to build pages), and theme authors (how to make those pages match your theme, which is optional). Skip to the section that applies to you.

Create a Twig view in your module. Extend the Module UI layout, and put your page inside the `module_content` block: ```twig {% extends "@core/module-layout.twig" %} {% block module_content %}

Hello from my module

This page is styled automatically.

Anything you put in here gets the theme's navbar and footer, plus Module UI styling.

A button
{% endblock %} ``` That is the whole idea. The rest of this page covers what each part does and every class you can use.

A module page is built from three layers of templates, each one extending the next:

```text
Your module view            e.g. @my-module/dashboard.twig
   |  extends
   v
@core/module-layout.twig    adds the Module UI stylesheet and a wrapper
   |  extends
   v
layouts/main.twig           the site's active theme: navbar, footer, fonts, colors
```

- Your view only contains the page itself.
- `@core/module-layout.twig` comes with the framework. It wraps your content in a `<div class="rhapsody-ui">` container, and adds the baseline stylesheet. Every Module UI rule is scoped to that container, so nothing leaks out and changes the rest of the theme.
- `layouts/main.twig` is whatever theme the site owner has chosen. Because your page extends it indirectly, you get that theme's navigation and footer for free, and you never need to know what they look like.

The stylesheet picks its colors from the surrounding text color instead of hard-coding a palette. That is why the same page works on a dark theme and a light theme without any extra work.

- `module_content`: your page goes here. This is the one you will use 99% of the time.
- `styles` and `scripts`: only if your page needs extra CSS or JavaScript. See the warning below.

Two easy mistakes:

- Do not override the `content` block. That block is where the wrapper and the Module UI classes live. Overriding it throws them away. Always use `module_content`.
- Always call `{{ parent() }}` when you override `styles` or `scripts`. Without it, the Module UI stylesheet or script is replaced by your block and your page loses its styling or spacing.

```twig
{% block scripts %}
    {{ parent() }}
    <script src="{{ base_url }}/my-module/chart.js"></script>
{% endblock %}
```
