{% endblock %} ```
For how your module's controller or route handler actually renders a view like this one, see the Modules documentation.

Themes position their navigation in all kinds of ways: a bar fixed to the top of the screen, a menu down the left side (very common in admin-style themes), a floating pill, or something else entirely. If a menu is fixed to the screen, it floats on top of the page, and content that starts at the very top of the page would be hidden underneath it.

Module UI handles this for you. A tiny script (loaded by `@core/module-layout.twig`) measures the page, finds any fixed menu that actually overlaps your content, and adds just enough padding to keep your page clear of it. It does not assume what kind of menu there is or how big it is.

- A wide, short bar at the top of the screen gets space added above your content.
- A tall, narrow menu on the left or right edge gets space added on that side.
- If the theme already leaves room for its menu, nothing extra is added.
- Menus that slide in and out (such as a mobile drawer), or collapse, are re-measured automatically when the window is resized or the menu animates.
- Things that are not navigation are ignored: cookie banners at the bottom, decorative backgrounds, and chat bubbles.

Good to know: this relies on JavaScript. If a visitor has it turned off, the page simply keeps its normal padding. The script also looks for menus that contain at least one link or button, which every real menu does.

If a theme has an unusual menu that is not detected correctly, the theme can set the space explicitly. See Customizing the look below.

Out of the box, Module UI works on any theme, and there is nothing you must do. If you would like module pages to match your theme more closely, set any of these CSS variables on `:root` in your theme's stylesheet. All of them are optional, and anything you leave out keeps its sensible default.

- `--rhapsody-primary`: the accent color, used for the main button, focus outlines and info alerts. Default: a violet-blue.
- `--rhapsody-primary-contrast`: the text color shown on top of the accent color. Default: white.
- `--rhapsody-danger`, `--rhapsody-success`, `--rhapsody-warning`: the red, green and amber used for errors, success messages and highlighted table cells.
- `--rhapsody-radius`: how rounded the corners are on cards, inputs and buttons. Default: `0.5rem`.
- `--rhapsody-gap`: the spacing between blocks. Default: `1rem`.
- `--rhapsody-border`: the color of borders and dividers.
- `--rhapsody-surface`: the background of cards and badges.
- `--rhapsody-inset-top`, `--rhapsody-inset-left`, `--rhapsody-inset-right`: space to reserve for a fixed menu. You normally do not need these, because the spacing is measured automatically. Use them only to override the automatic result. The larger of the two values wins.

For example, a theme with a gold accent and square corners might add this to its main stylesheet:

```css
:root {
    --rhapsody-primary: #c9a227;
    --rhapsody-primary-contrast: #1a1a1a;
    --rhapsody-radius: 2px;
}
```

The default border and card colors are worked out from the text color, so they already suit both light and dark themes. Most themes only need to set `--rhapsody-primary` to feel at home.

- Using the theme's own classes. Classes like Tailwind's `bg-blue-500` only exist if the active theme provides them. A module cannot know that. Stick to `rhapsody-*` classes and your page works everywhere.
- Putting Module UI classes outside `module_content`. The styles only apply inside the `rhapsody-ui` wrapper, which `module_content` sits in.
- Overriding `content` instead of `module_content`. This removes the wrapper and the styling.
- Forgetting `{{ parent() }}` when overriding `styles` or `scripts`.
- Hard-coding URLs such as `/my-module/save`. Use `{{ base_url }}/my-module/save` so your module works when the site is installed in a sub-folder.
- Forgetting `{{ csrf_field()|raw }}` inside a form.

Modules are installable Composer packages that add functionality to your Rhapsody site — event listeners, routes, Twig helpers, admin-configurable settings. You can build them for your own use, share them privately, or sell them on the Rhapsody Marketplace.

Key concept: a module's code never runs freely. Instead, it receives a `ModuleContext` object that acts as a controlled gateway. Every action you take through this gateway is checked against your module's `module.json` manifest — if you haven't declared a capability, the action is denied immediately.

If you already know what a service container, a Composer package, and PSR-4 autoloading are, skip to Module Structure. If any of those are new to you, read this section — everything else on this page assumes you understand them.

Rhapsody, like most modern PHP frameworks, is built around a service container (sometimes called a "dependency injection container," or just "the container"). It's a single object, built once per request, that knows how to construct and hand out every major piece of the framework — the `Router`, the `EventDispatcher`, the Twig `Environment`, your database connection, and so on.

The reason this exists: without it, every class that needs a Router would have to know how to build one itself — including all of its dependencies, and their dependencies, all the way down. The container does that wiring once, centrally, and anything that needs a piece of the framework just asks the container for it by type. Framework code (controllers, core services) does this constantly. For example, deep inside the framework, something like this happens on every request:

```php
$router = $container->resolve(Router::class);
$twig   = $container->resolve(Environment::class);
```

That's normal, everyday framework code. It is not something your module ever does directly, and that's deliberate — read on.

headingPath: Why modules don't get the container
chunks.text:
If a module could call `$container->resolve(...)` for anything it wanted, it could reach the database connection, read `$_SERVER`, register global middleware that intercepts every request on the site, or call `exec()`. At that point, reviewing a module before it goes on the marketplace means reading every single line of its code, by hand, forever — there's no way to reason about what it might do just by reading its manifest.

So modules don't get the container. Instead, every module's entry point receives a `ModuleContext` object — a small, deliberately limited stand-in. `ModuleContext` hands out exactly five focused tools (we call them facades — a facade here just means "a small wrapper object that stands between your code and a real framework service, and checks your permissions before doing anything on your behalf"). You'll meet all five in section 5.

This is the single most important idea on this page: your module's code never touches the container, the database, or the filesystem directly — it only ever talks to `$context`, and `$context` checks your manifest before doing anything.

headingPath: What is a Composer package, briefly
chunks.text: If you've used PHP for any length of time you've probably run `composer require` for something. A module is exactly that kind of package — a directory with a `composer.json` describing its name, its dependencies, and (critically for autoloading — see below) which folder its PHP classes live in. Nothing about a Rhapsody module is a special new packaging format; it's a normal Composer package with one extra convention (a `module.json` manifest) and one required field (`"type": "rhapsody-module"`) that tells Rhapsody's module system to look for it.

A module is a standard Composer package with one special requirement: its `type` must be `rhapsody-module`. That's the field Rhapsody's `ModuleRegistry` uses to find your package among everything else installed in `vendor/` — it asks Composer, "give me every installed package whose type is exactly `rhapsody-module`," and goes from there.

```bash
my-modules/welcome-bonus/
├── composer.json      # Standard Composer file
├── module.json        # Your module's manifest (most important file!)
└── src/
    └── ModuleProvider.php  # Your module's entry point
```

Here's a minimal `composer.json`:

```json
{
    "name": "acme/welcome-bonus",
    "type": "rhapsody-module",
    "require": {
        "php": "^8.3",
        "arout/rhapsody-core": "^2.0"
    },
    "autoload": {
        "psr-4": { "Acme\\WelcomeBonus\\": "src/" }
    }
}
```

Walking through every line, for anyone new to `composer.json`:

- `name` — the package name Composer (and Rhapsody) identify this module by. Always `vendor-slug/module-slug`, lowercase.
- `type` — must be exactly `rhapsody-module`. This is not a Rhapsody-specific Composer feature — `type` is a standard Composer field any package can set to any string; Rhapsody's `ModuleRegistry` just happens to look specifically for this value.
- `require` — your module's own dependencies. You'll basically always require `arout/rhapsody-core` with a version constraint, since your code depends on classes like `ModuleContext` that live in that package.
- `autoload` — the PSR-4 mapping explained above.

This file declares everything your module is allowed to do. Think of it as a permission request form, filled out once, that the framework checks against for the entire lifetime of your module. If your provider ever tries to do something not listed here, the framework throws an exception immediately — no silent failures, no security holes, and (this matters a lot once you submit to the marketplace) no need for a human reviewer to read your whole codebase just to know what your module is capable of. They can read this one file.

- `name` – `vendor-slug/module-slug`, must match your Composer package name exactly, character for character.
- `type` – must be `"rhapsody-module"`. Same field as in `composer.json`, repeated here so the manifest is self-describing even outside a Composer context.
- `version` – semantic version, e.g. `1.0.0`. (If "semantic version" is new to you: it's the `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` convention where you bump `MAJOR` for breaking changes, `MINOR` for new backward-compatible features, and `PATCH` for bug fixes.)
- `rhapsody_core` – a version constraint against the installed core, e.g. `"^2.0"` means "any 2.x version, but not 3.0 or later." Modules whose constraint doesn't match the installed core version are skipped gracefully at boot — not a fatal error, just quietly not loaded, with a line in the error log explaining why.
- `title` – human-readable name displayed in the marketplace and in `module:list` output. This is what a person sees, as opposed to `name`, which is what the machine sees.
- `provider` – the fully-qualified class name of your entry-point class (see Writing the Provider), e.g. `"Acme\\WelcomeBonus\\ModuleProvider"`. Note the doubled backslashes — that's how a single literal backslash is written inside a JSON string.

- `description` – shown on your marketplace listing. Keep it to a sentence or two.
- `category` – must be one of: `seo`, `commerce`, `content`, `analytics`, `integration`, `security`, `media`, `utility`, `other`. Defaults to `other` if you leave it out.
- `license` – an SPDX identifier (like `MIT`) or `proprietary` for a commercial license. Defaults to `proprietary`.
- `author` – an object with optional `name`, `email`, `url` sub-fields.
- `settings_schema` – defines the fields for an admin-editable settings form (validated today; the actual form-rendering UI is planned but not shipped yet — see What's Coming). Write it anyway; when the renderer ships, your module gets a working settings page for free with no code changes.

There are exactly seven capability keys, and this is a closed list — you cannot invent an eighth, and putting anything else here fails validation. Omitting a key (or explicitly setting it to `false`) means your module cannot perform that action, full stop; there's no "maybe" or "ask at runtime." Each one is covered in exhaustive detail in section 5 below, but as a quick preview, they are: `events.listen`, `routes.register`, `twig.extensions`, `twig.functions`, `storage.access`, `settings.manage`, `database.access`.

```json
{
    "name": "acme/welcome-bonus",
    "type": "rhapsody-module",
    "version": "1.0.0",
    "rhapsody_core": "^2.0",
    "title": "Welcome Bonus",
    "description": "Grants new users a configurable welcome bonus.",
    "category": "commerce",
    "provider": "Acme\\WelcomeBonus\\ModuleProvider",
    "permissions": {
        "events.listen": { "listen": ["Rhapsody\\Core\\Events\\UserRegistered"] },
        "routes.register": { "prefix": "welcome-bonus" },
        "settings.manage": {},
        "storage.access": {}
    },
    "settings_schema": [
        { "key": "bonus_amount", "type": "number", "label": "Bonus amount (USD)", "default": 10 }
    ]
}
```

Notice this module did not declare `twig.extensions`, `twig.functions`, or a wide-open `events.listen` — it only asked for exactly what it uses. That's the pattern to copy: request the smallest set of permissions your module actually needs. It's not just tidiness — a smaller permission set is faster to review and more likely to sail through automated marketplace checks without a human needing to look at it at all.

Important: an invalid manifest (unknown permission key, malformed field, missing required field) throws a `ManifestValidationException` the moment it's parsed. During normal boot, this disables just that one module — logged, not fatal, the rest of your site keeps working. During marketplace submission, manifest validation is the very first, cheapest stage of the automated review pipeline, run before a single line of your module's actual PHP code is ever executed.

Some real examples of what that exception message actually looks like, so you can recognize it instantly if you hit it:

```text
module.json: missing required field "provider"
module.json: "type" must be "rhapsody-module", got "plugin"
module.json: "name" must look like "vendor-slug/module-slug"
module.json: "version" must be valid semver, got "1.0"
module.json: unknown permission "payments.charge" — allowed: events.listen, routes.register, twig.extensions, twig.functions, storage.access, settings.manage, database.access
module.json: "events.listen" requires a non-empty "listen" array of event class names
```

Each of those corresponds to exactly one thing going wrong — a typo'd field name, a permission key that doesn't exist, forgetting the `listen` array. If you see one of these, the fix is almost always a one-line edit to `module.json`.

Your provider class is the entry point for your module — the one class the framework ever directly instantiates and calls into. It must implement three methods from `ModuleServiceProviderInterface`:

- `boot()` – runs on every request, for every module that's currently installed. This is where you register listeners, routes, and Twig helpers. Keep it fast — it's on the hot path of every single page load.
- `install()` – runs exactly once, the first time an operator runs `php rhapsody module:install your/module`. Seed default settings here, create database tables (once that capability ships), anything that should happen one time on activation.
- `uninstall()` – runs exactly once, when an operator runs `php rhapsody module:uninstall your/module`. Clean up whatever `install()` created.

To make the "runs on every request" vs. "runs once" distinction concrete, here's the actual sequence of events, from Composer installing your package to your code executing on a real page load:

```bash
composer require acme/welcome-bonus     # code is on disk, autoloadable — nothing runs yet
php rhapsody module:list                # ModuleRegistry finds it (type: rhapsody-module), shows "not installed"
php rhapsody module:install acme/welcome-bonus
    → ModuleRegistry validates the manifest
    → ModuleRegistry checks rhapsody_core compatibility
    → your provider's install() runs — ONCE, right now
    → the module is marked "installed"

# every request from here on, e.g. a browser hitting any page of the site:
    → bootstrap.php builds the container
    → ModuleRegistry::bootAll() runs
    → for every INSTALLED module (yours included): your provider's boot() runs
    → your event listeners / routes / twig helpers are now live for this request
    → the rest of the request is handled normally (routing, controller, response)

php rhapsody module:uninstall acme/welcome-bonus --force
    → your provider's uninstall() runs — ONCE, right now
    → the module is marked "not installed" — boot() will not run for it anymore
```

The practical upshot: nothing in your module does anything at all until an operator explicitly runs `module:install`. Being `composer require`'d only makes your module discoverable, not active.

Here's a complete, real provider (this is the actual `acme/welcome-bonus` example module shipped with the framework — you can find it at `vendor/arout/rhapsody-core/examples/acme-welcome-bonus/` and read/copy it directly):

1. `$context->events()->listen(UserRegistered::class, ...)` — registers a closure to run whenever a `UserRegistered` event is dispatched anywhere in the application. The closure itself receives the event object.
2. Inside that closure, `$context->settings()->get('bonus_amount', 10)` reads a setting, falling back to `10` if it was never set.
3. `$context->storage()->put(...)` writes a line to a log file that belongs exclusively to this module.
4. `$context->routes()->get('/balance', ...)` registers an HTTP route. Because this module's manifest sets `"prefix": "welcome-bonus"`, the final URL is `/welcome-bonus/balance`, not just `/balance` — more on exactly how that path gets built in 4.2.

Golden Rule: everything goes through `$context` — never reach for the service container, raw PDO, `$_SERVER`, `eval()`, or system functions like `exec()` directly. Marketplace static analysis specifically looks for exactly these patterns and will flag a submission that uses them, regardless of intent.

`$context` — the single argument every one of your three provider methods receives — is an instance of `Rhapsody\Core\Modules\ModuleContext`. It doesn't do much on its own; its entire job is to hand you one of six small, focused objects (the "facades" from section 1) when you call a method on it:

```php
$context->events()    // → EventsFacade
$context->routes()    // → RoutesFacade
$context->twig()      // → TwigFacade
$context->storage()   // → StorageFacade
$context->settings()  // → SettingsFacade
$context->database()  // → DatabaseFacade
```

Every single one of these facades does the same thing before doing anything else: it checks `ModulePermissions::can('the.relevant.key')` against your manifest. If the answer is no, it throws `ModulePermissionException` immediately — your code never even reaches the real framework service underneath. This check happens on every call, not just once at boot, so there's no way to "get away with it" by calling something in an unusual order.

First, what an "event" actually is, if that's a new concept: an event is a small object representing "something already happened" — a user registered, a payment succeeded — broadcast to anyone who cares, without the code that dispatched it needing to know who (if anyone) is listening. This is what lets your module react to things happening elsewhere in the application without the application needing to know your module exists.

As of this version of the framework, there are exactly four events dispatched by core that a module can listen for:

Event class | Dispatched when | Public properties
`Rhapsody\Core\Events\UserRegistered` | A new user finishes registration | `$event->user` — the new `User` entity
`Rhapsody\Core\Events\PaymentSucceededEvent` | A payment completes successfully | `$event->transactionId`, `$event->amount`, `$event->metadata`
`Rhapsody\Core\Events\PaymentFailedEvent` | A payment attempt fails | `$event->message`, `$event->context`
`Rhapsody\Core\Events\RouteNotFound`* | No registered route matches the incoming request | `$event->uri`, `$event->method` — plus a `setResponse(Response $response)` method

1. `EventsFacade::listen()` checks `$this->permissions->can('events.listen')`. If `events.listen` isn't in your manifest at all, it throws immediately: `Module "your-slug" tried to listen for events without declaring "events.listen" in module.json`.
2. It then checks that the specific event class you passed is in your declared whitelist. If it isn't, it throws: `Module "your-slug" tried to listen for "SomeOther\Event", which isn't in its declared events.listen.listen whitelist`.
3. Only if both checks pass does it call the real `EventDispatcher::listen()` underneath — the same dispatcher core itself uses.

Lets you read and write files that belong exclusively to your module.

```php
$context->storage()->put('log.txt', "Some data\n");           // write (creates or overwrites)
$content = $context->storage()->get('log.txt');                // read — returns false if missing
$exists  = $context->storage()->exists('log.txt');              // check without reading
$context->storage()->delete('log.txt');                         // remove
```

Every path you pass is resolved relative to `storage/modules/{your-slug}/` — for the `acme/welcome-bonus` example above, that's literally `storage/modules/acme-welcome-bonus/` on disk. You never construct that path yourself; you just pass `'log.txt'` or `'cache/report.json'` and the facade does the rest.

Path traversal is actively blocked, not just discouraged. If you pass something like `'../../.env'`, trying to reach outside your module's own directory, the facade resolves the real filesystem path and checks it's still inside your sandbox before touching the disk — if it isn't, it throws `ModulePermissionException` with the message `Storage path escapes module sandbox: ../../.env` rather than silently succeeding. There is no way to read or write anything outside your own module's storage folder through this facade, full stop.

Typical uses: application logs specific to your module, generated/cached files (a rendered report, a downloaded image), simple flat-file data that doesn't need a real database table.

Lets your module persist its own configuration — the kind of thing an admin would eventually edit in a settings screen (see `settings_schema` back in section 3).

```php
$context->settings()->set('bonus_amount', 25);              // write — requires settings.manage
$amount = $context->settings()->get('bonus_amount', 10);    // read — always allowed, even without the permission
$all    = $context->settings()->all();                       // every setting as an array
```

This is the one asymmetric permission on this whole page. Every other facade gates the entire capability — but for settings, reads are always allowed, with or without `settings.manage` declared, because a module obviously needs to read its own configuration just to function. Only writing a new value requires the permission.

How this is actually stored, in full: under the hood, each module's settings live in one plain JSON file, at `storage/modules/{your-slug}/settings.json`. For the welcome-bonus example, after `install()` has run, that file looks exactly like this on disk:

```json
{
    "bonus_amount": 10
}
```

Every `set()` call reads that whole file, updates the one key you're setting, and writes the whole file back out — so it's safe to call `set()` repeatedly with different keys over time; nothing gets clobbered. There's no schema enforcement at the storage layer itself — you can store a string, a number, an array, whatever `json_encode()` can represent — but your `settings_schema` declaration is what tells the (future) admin UI what type each field should be and how to render it.

This is a JSON file rather than a database table by design, and that's not just a historical accident from before `database.access` existed — it keeps a module's own configuration readable and versionable as a single small file, with no schema migration of its own to manage. If your module needs genuinely relational storage instead (multiple rows, foreign keys, querying by anything other than a settings key), that's exactly what `database.access` below is for — the two are complementary, not one superseding the other.

Method | Scope | Notes
`query($sql, $params)` | Any table, read-only | Must start with `SELECT`/`WITH`; a write-like keyword found anywhere else in the string is rejected too, as a defense against a stacked statement slipping through.
`select($table, $where)` | Any table, read-only | A structured convenience wrapper for the common case — no need to hand-write SQL for a simple lookup.
`insert() / update() / delete()` | Your tables only | Table name is a real parameter, not embedded in a SQL string — checked with a plain string comparison against your prefix, not parsed out of free-form SQL.
`migrate($sql)` | Your tables only | Accepts `CREATE TABLE`, `ALTER TABLE`, or `DROP TABLE` only — this is how a module gets its own real tables in the first place. Call it from `install()` to create, `uninstall()` to drop.
`find() / findBy()` | Any entity, read-only | Doctrine equivalent of `query()` — works against any entity the application already has mapped, e.g. `Rhapsody\Core\Entities\User`.
`save() / remove()` | Your entities only | Checked via Doctrine's own metadata — `getClassMetadata($entity)->getTableName()` — against your prefix before `persist()`/`flush()` is allowed to run.

Notice `$context->database()` never hands you a raw `PDO` connection or the application's actual `EntityManager` — on purpose. Either one would come with unrestricted `exec()` or unrestricted `persist()` on any entity, which would make every other rule in this section decorative. Everything above is the entire surface area; if something isn't listed here, `DatabaseFacade` doesn't do it.

While you're building a module, you don't want to publish it anywhere just to test it. Point your app's Composer at the module's local folder with a path repository:

```json
// your-app/composer.json
"repositories": [
    { "type": "path", "url": "../my-modules/welcome-bonus" }
],
"require": {
    "acme/welcome-bonus": "*"
}
```

This tells Composer "treat this local folder as if it were a real registered package," so you can iterate on the module's code and just re-run Composer to pick up changes, with no publishing step.

Composer installation (getting the code) and module activation (making it run) are two separate, deliberate steps — this trips up almost everyone the first time:

```bash
# 1. Get the code
composer update acme/welcome-bonus

# 2. See everything Composer/Rhapsody can discover
php rhapsody module:list
#   acme/welcome-bonus     v1.0.0     not installed

# 3. Actually activate it (runs install(), boot() will now run every request)
php rhapsody module:install acme/welcome-bonus
#   "acme/welcome-bonus" v1.0.0 installed and activated.

php rhapsody module:list
#   acme/welcome-bonus     v1.0.0     installed
```

- Routes — just hit them with `curl` or your browser: `curl http://your-app.test/welcome-bonus/balance`. No special setup needed.
- Event listeners — trigger the actual event through your application's real flow (e.g. registering a user through the real signup form), not by inserting a row directly into the database. Events only fire where application code explicitly dispatches them — a raw database insert never touches that code path, so your listener simply won't run.
- Settings — after `install()` has run, check `storage/modules/{your-slug}/settings.json` directly. You can hand-edit it during testing to simulate an admin changing a setting, then re-test your module's behavior.
- Storage — check files under `storage/modules/{your-slug}/` directly with `cat`/a file browser after triggering whatever writes to them.

Command | What it does
`module:list` | Lists every module Composer can discover (any installed package of type `rhapsody-module`) and whether it's currently installed.
`module:install {name}` | Runs `install()` once and activates the module. Fails if the core-version constraint doesn't match, the provider class can't be found, or `install()` itself throws. Running it again on an already-installed module is a safe no-op — it won't re-run `install()`.
`module:uninstall {name} [--force]` | Runs `uninstall()` and deactivates the module. Prompts for confirmation first (since `uninstall()` may delete data) unless `--force`/`-f` is passed.

Note: `module:uninstall` does not remove the package from `vendor/` — that's a separate, deliberate step if you also want the code itself gone:

```bash
php rhapsody module:uninstall acme/welcome-bonus --force
composer remove acme/welcome-bonus
```

The welcome-bonus example above touches four of the six facades but keeps each one simple. For a module that leans harder into `routes.register` — using both namespacing styles, `root()`, and `registered()` in one place — read through `acme/seo-toolkit`, also shipped with the framework at `vendor/arout/rhapsody-core/examples/acme-seo-toolkit/`. It generates `sitemap.xml` and `robots.txt` entirely from the live route table, configurable through settings, with zero database dependency and zero manually-maintained URL list. Its manifest:

That last filter — excluding by `$route->controller` — is worth calling out specifically: it's what lets this module tell apart core's own internal `/docs/*` reference pages (handled by `Rhapsody\Core\Controllers\DocsController`) from an app's own `/docs` pages under a completely different controller class, even though both sit at the same URL prefix. Path matching alone can't make that distinction — you need the actual handler identity, which is exactly what `RegisteredRoute::$controller` gives you.
Real errors you'll actually hit while building a module, and what they mean.

- Did you run `php rhapsody module:install your/module`? Routes are only registered inside `boot()`, and `boot()` only runs for installed modules. Check with `module:list`.
- Did you declare `routes.register` in your manifest at all?
- Remember the automatic prefix — `$context->routes()->get('/balance', ...)` is not at `/balance`, it's at `/{your-prefix}/balance`. Double-check the URL you're actually requesting.

This always means the same thing: your code called a facade method for a capability your manifest didn't declare — or declared, but not broadly enough (e.g. an event class not in your `listen` whitelist, or a root path not in your `paths` whitelist). The exception message names exactly which permission and which action. Fix: add or widen the relevant block in `module.json`.

Your `module.json` itself is malformed — a typo'd field name, an unknown permission key, a missing required field, an invalid semver string. The exception message quotes the exact field and rule that failed (see the examples in section 3). Fix the JSON file directly; this has nothing to do with your PHP code.

headingPath: "My provider class isn't found" / module doesn't show up in module:list
chunks.text:
- Almost always a PSR-4 mismatch — re-check the autoloading explanation above. The `provider` field in `module.json` must exactly match a real, autoloadable class.
- Confirm `"type": "rhapsody-module"` is set in both `composer.json` and `module.json` — it's genuinely required in both places, for different reasons (Composer package discovery vs. manifest validation).
- After any change to `composer.json`'s autoload block, run `composer dump-autoload`. If your project's Composer is configured with an optimized/cached autoloader, new classes added to an existing package might not be picked up until you regenerate it.

- Confirm you triggered the event through the real application flow, not a direct database write — see section 6.
- Confirm the module is actually installed ( `module:list`) — `boot()`, where `listen()` is called, only runs for installed modules.
- Double-check the event class name in your manifest's `listen` array matches exactly, including the full namespace.

- Confirm you declared `settings.manage` — without it, `set()` throws rather than silently failing, so check your error log/output for a `ModulePermissionException`.
- Check `storage/modules/{your-slug}/settings.json` directly to see the actual current state on disk — this sidesteps any question of whether your code is reading the value you think it's reading.

- First check the message itself — it tells you which of two things went wrong: missing `database.access` entirely, or a table name that doesn't start with your prefix. They're different fixes.
- Remember reads need the permission too. Unlike `settings.manage`, forgetting to declare `database.access` breaks `query()`/ `select()`/ `find()` just as much as it breaks a write.
- Your table prefix is always `mod_` + your manifest's `name` field with `/` and `-` both converted to `_` — e.g. `acme/click-tracker` becomes `mod_acme_click_tracker_`. If your table doesn't start with exactly that, `insert()`/ `update()`/ `delete()`/ `migrate()`/ `save()`/ `remove()` will all reject it — there's no way to configure or override the prefix.
- For a Doctrine entity specifically, the check runs against the table name in your entity's own `#[ORM\Table(name: ...)]` attribute, not the entity's class name — a mismatched attribute is the usual cause here.

Module

A Composer package of type `rhapsody-module` that adds functionality to a Rhapsody site through the permission-based API described on this page.

Manifest

The `module.json` file — declares what a module is and what it's allowed to do. See section 3.

Provider

The class named in a manifest's `provider` field — a module's entry point, implementing `boot()`, `install()`, and `uninstall()`.

Slug

A module's `name` field with the slash replaced by a dash — `acme/welcome-bonus` becomes `acme-welcome-bonus`. Used to namespace routes, scoped storage, and settings so modules can never collide with each other.

Capability / Permission

One of the seven fixed keys in a manifest's `permissions` block, each unlocking one facade method (or part of one).

Facade (as used on this page)

A small object (`EventsFacade`, `RoutesFacade`, etc.) that stands between your module's code and a real framework service, checking your manifest's permissions before doing anything. Not the same concept as a "Laravel Facade," if you've encountered that term elsewhere — no static magic methods here, just plain objects.

Service Container ("the container")

The object, built once per request, that constructs and hands out every major framework service (`Router`, `EventDispatcher`, the Twig `Environment`, etc.). Modules never access it directly — see section 1.

Composer package

A directory with a `composer.json`, installable via `composer require`. Every Rhapsody module is one, with the extra `"type": "rhapsody-module"` field.

PSR-4 autoloading

The standard that maps a PHP namespace onto a folder structure, so class files load automatically without manual `require` statements. Configured per-package in `composer.json`'s `autoload.psr-4` block.

Semver (semantic versioning)

The `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` version numbering convention (e.g. `1.4.2`), and the constraint syntax built on it (e.g. `^2.0` means "2.x, not 3.0+") used in both `version` and `rhapsody_core`.

Twig

The templating language Rhapsody themes are written in (the `.twig` files under `views/themes/`). `twig.extensions`/`twig.functions` let a module add logic theme authors can call from a template.

Future capabilities on the roadmap:

- Admin UI renderer – automatically generate a working settings form from `settings_schema`, no extra code required.
- Global middleware – for modules that need to intercept every request (e.g. a maintenance-mode module), deliberately not available yet since it's the single most powerful capability a module could have.

The manifest schema already reserves space for all of these, so adopting them later won't break any existing `module.json` file you write today.

- Modules are Composer packages with `type: "rhapsody-module"`, discovered via `Composer\InstalledVersions`.
- The manifest (`module.json`) declares permissions – only what's listed is allowed; seven fixed capability keys, no exceptions.
- The provider is the entry point – implements `boot()` (every request), `install()` (once, on activation), `uninstall()` (once, on deactivation).
- Everything goes through `$context` – never the raw container, never a raw `PDO` connection or `EntityManager`, never `$_SERVER`/ `exec()` directly; use `$context->database()` for scoped database access.
- Composer install ≠ module activation – `module:install` is what actually turns a module on.
- Namespaced routes are auto-prefixed with your slug; use `root()` plus an explicit `paths` whitelist for true root-level URLs.
- `routes()->registered()` gives read-only access to the live route table, gated by the same `routes.register` permission.
- Storage is sandboxed to `storage/modules/{slug}/`, with path traversal actively blocked.
- Settings are JSON-file-backed at `storage/modules/{slug}/settings.json` — reads always allowed, writes require `settings.manage`.
- Database access is table-namespace-scoped — read any table, but write only to your own `mod_{slug}_*` tables (row data via `insert()`/ `update()`/ `delete()`, schema via `migrate()`); unlike settings, reads also require `database.access`.
- Twig function names are auto-prefixed `mod_{slug}_` to prevent collisions.
- Request only the permissions you actually use — smaller manifests review faster, both by automation and by humans.

Rhapsody includes a `Rhapsody\Core\Pagination` class that makes breaking large datasets into navigable pages straightforward, with optional support for custom CSS classes, a custom base URL, windowed page ranges with First/Last links, a jump-to-page menu, AJAX-friendly data attributes, and rendering through your own Twig template.

In your Twig template, call the `render()` method on the pagination object. It takes no arguments and returns a ready-to-use HTML string: ```twig
{{ pagination.render()|raw }}
``` The rendered markup is a `
` containing a Previous link, a link for every page number, and a Next link — with the current page shown as inactive text rather than a link, and Previous/Next shown as disabled text at the start/end of the range. If there's only one page total, `render()` returns an empty string.

`setCssClasses()` accepts any subset of the following keys — anything you don't override keeps its default value, which matches the framework's original unstyled markup exactly, so calling code that never touches this method sees no visual change:

- `container` – wraps the whole nav in a `<div>` with this class (only added if you set a non-empty value)
- `list` – class on the `<ul>`
- `item` – class on each `<li>`
- `link` – class on each clickable page link
- `disabled` – class on the disabled Previous/Next text
- `active` – class on the current page's text

Any query parameters already present on the current request (other than `page`) are carried forward onto every page link automatically — for example, if the page was requested with `?limit=25&sort=name`, every rendered link will include `&limit=25&sort=name` as well. This happens automatically by reading the current request's query string; there's no method to add parameters that aren't already part of it.

In addition to the keys from section 4, `setCssClasses()` now also accepts:

- `ellipsis` – the "…" shown between a First/Last link and the windowed page range
- `jumpForm` – the jump-to-page `<form>`
- `jumpLabel` – the "Jump to page:" `<label>`
- `jumpMenu` – the `<select>` itself
- `jumpButton` – the "Go" fallback `<button>`

Combine `toAjaxPayload()` with `Request::wantsJson()` to get near-instant page transitions on a rapidly changing dataset, without giving up a fast, fully-rendered initial page load or risking stale cached HTML — the same controller and the same route serve both the normal page load and the AJAX request, so there's no separate API endpoint or duplicated list-rendering logic to maintain.

`data-list-target`, `data-pagination-target`, and `data-jump-target` tell the script which elements to swap — the last is optional, only needed when `setShowJumpMenu(true)` is in use: ```twig
{{ listHtml|raw }}
{{ pagination.render({showJumpMenu: false})|raw }}
{{ pagination.renderJumpMenu()|raw }}
``` Progressive by design: every link in `render()`'s output is a real, fully-working `href`, and the jump-menu is a real `
` — with JavaScript disabled (or before the script has finished loading) the page just navigates normally. The script only intercepts what it can enhance.

Hard-coded and relative paths are one of the most common sources of “works on my machine” bugs. `Path` removes the whole category:

- Independent of the working directory. A relative path like `'storage/logs/app.log'` is resolved against the current working directory, which is not the same for a web request, a CLI command, a cron job, or a persistent worker. `Path` always starts from your project root.
- No `../../../` chains. Moving a file to another folder never silently breaks the paths inside it.
- Cross-platform. Slashes in the path you pass in are normalised to the operating system's native separator, so the same code works on Windows (WAMP), Linux, and macOS.
- One source of truth. If a directory ever moves, there is one place to update, not dozens of string literals.

Every method accepts an optional `$path` string that is appended to the directory.

Method | Resolves to
`Path::root()` | The application root (the folder that contains `vendor/`)
`Path::app()` | `app/` – your controllers, models, and other application code
`Path::config()` | `config/`
`Path::public()` | `public/` – used to store CSS / JS and images
`Path::storage()` | `storage/`
`Path::cache()` | `storage/cache/`
`Path::logs()` | `storage/logs/`
`Path::resources()` | `resources/`
`Path::views()` | `views/`
`Path::database()` | `db/` – migrations, seeds, and similar files (note the folder is named `db`, not `database`)

- Results never end with a separator, with or without a sub-path. Pass the entire sub-path as the argument rather than concatenating pieces yourself.
- Forward and backward slashes in the argument are converted to the OS's native separator.
- Leading slashes in the argument are stripped, so `Path::config('/mail.php')` and `Path::config('mail.php')` are identical. A leading slash does not mean “the root of the server's disk”.
- `Path` only builds strings. It does not check that the file exists and does not create missing folders.

chunks.text:
Every other method is built on `Path::root()`, which determines the base directory like this:

1. If a `ROOT_DIR` constant is defined, it is used. The application's `public/index.php` defines this for you.
2. Otherwise `Path` falls back to walking up from its own location inside `vendor/arout/rhapsody-core/src/Helpers/` to the project root.

With a standard install you never need to think about this. If you use a non-standard directory layout, define `ROOT_DIR` in your entry point before the framework boots and every `Path` method will follow it.

Because the fallback relies on the package living inside `vendor/`, make sure `ROOT_DIR` is defined in any custom entry script that runs from somewhere unusual (for example a standalone CLI or worker script).

Rhapsody includes several caching layers designed to significantly improve your application's speed and responsiveness, especially in a production environment. Understanding and utilizing these features is key to building a high-performance application. Caching is primarily managed through the Rhapsody Console.

The framework supports multiple cache backends, or "drivers." You can switch between them with a single configuration change in your `.env` file.

```bash
# Use the local filesystem for caching
CACHE_DRIVER=file

# Use a Redis server for caching
CACHE_DRIVER=redis
```

The cache is managed by the `Rhapsody\Core\Cache` class, which is available via the service container. You should inject it into your controller's constructor. The most common way to interact with the cache is the `remember()` method.

Once injected, you can use other methods on your `$this->cache` instance:

- `$this->cache->get('key')`: Retrieve an item from the cache.
- `$this->cache->put('key', $value, $minutes)`: Store an item in the cache.
- `$this->cache->has('key')`: Check if an item exists in the cache.
- `$this->cache->forget('key')`: Remove an item from the cache.

Twig compiles templates into plain PHP files for faster rendering. In production, you should pre‑compile all templates to avoid the overhead of compilation on the fly. Rhapsody provides a console command to do this:

```bash
php rhapsody app:cache-warm
```

This command scans all your theme and core view directories, compiles every `.twig` template, and stores the compiled PHP files in the cache directory (usually `storage/cache/views`).

Run this command after deploying your application or after making changes to your templates. It ensures that your users experience the fastest possible response times.

You can also clear the compiled template cache with:

```bash
php rhapsody cache:clear
```

This removes all compiled templates, forcing Twig to recompile them on the next request (useful during development).

For high‑traffic applications, you can cache your route definitions to speed up routing. Generate a route cache with:

```bash
php rhapsody route:cache
```

This compiles all your routes into a PHP file that the router loads directly, bypassing the need to parse your route files on every request. Clear the route cache with:

```bash
php rhapsody route:clear
```

Tip: In production, run `cache:clear` and `route:cache` as part of your deployment script to ensure optimal performance.

A persistent queue is a background task management system that detaches time-consuming operations from the main web request-response cycle. The queue runs work in the background, outside the web request. Instead of holding transient job data solely in volatile memory (RAM), a persistent queue stores jobs reliably in non-volatile storage (such as your database or a dedicated disk-backed store). Because jobs are durably saved, they survive application crashes or server restarts, automatically handle retries upon failure, and can be distributed safely across one or multiple background worker processes.

- Fault Tolerance & Durability: If a worker crashes mid-task or the entire server goes down, the job remains safely stored. Once the system recovers, it resumes processing without data loss.
- Asynchronous Execution: Heavy tasks run in the background, allowing your web application to respond instantly to users without making them wait for slow operations to finish.
- Load Leveling & Traffic Spikes: Queues act as a buffer during high-traffic surges, catching incoming jobs and feeding them to your workers at a steady, manageable pace so your database and external APIs don't get overwhelmed.
- Independent Scalability: You can scale your web servers and your background worker pools independently depending on where your resource bottlenecks lie.

headingPath: When to Use Them (Common Use Cases)

chunks.text:
A job is a small class that implements `JobInterface` and has a public `handle()` method.

- `handle()` gets its dependencies from the container. Type-hint the services you need, exactly as you would in a controller. The worker calls it through `Container::call()`, so aliases, singletons and closure bindings all apply.
- The constructor holds what you dispatch with. Pass plain values: an id, a string, a number. Look the full record up inside `handle()` so the job always works with fresh data.
- No closures or open resources in constructor arguments. The job is stored as text, and a job that cannot be stored is refused when you dispatch it, with a message naming the class.

If `handle()` throws, the job is put back and tried again after a wait. When it runs out of attempts it moves to the failed jobs. Tune this per job with attributes:

```php
use Rhapsody\Core\Queue\Attributes\Backoff;
use Rhapsody\Core\Queue\Attributes\Timeout;
use Rhapsody\Core\Queue\Attributes\Tries;

#[Tries(5)]       // give up after 5 attempts
#[Backoff(30)]    // wait 30s, then 60s, 120s, 240s
#[Timeout(45)]    // abort an attempt that runs longer than 45s
final class ImportCatalog implements JobInterface { /* ... */ }
```

Attribute | Default | What it does
`#[Tries(int $times)]` | 3 | Total attempts, including the first.
`#[Backoff(int $seconds, bool $exponential = true)]` | 10s, doubling | Wait before a retry. With `exponential: false` the wait is always the same. Capped at one day.
`#[Timeout(int $seconds)]` | 60s | Longest an attempt may run. A job that exceeds it counts as a failed attempt. Needs the `pcntl` extension (see Good to Know).

```bash
php rhapsody queue:work                          # process the "default" queue
php rhapsody queue:work --queue=high,default     # "high" is always checked first
php rhapsody queue:work --stop-when-empty        # drain the queue, then exit
```

Option | Default | Meaning
`--queue=a,b` (`-q`) | `default` | Queues to process, in priority order. A later queue is only looked at when the earlier ones are empty.
`--sleep=N` | 3 | Seconds to wait when every queue is empty.
`--max-jobs=N` | 0 (no limit) | Stop after this many jobs.
`--max-time=N` | 0 (no limit) | Stop after this many seconds. Checked between jobs.
`--memory=MB` | 128 | Stop once memory use reaches this many megabytes, so a supervisor can start a fresh worker.
`--stop-when-empty` | off | Exit as soon as every queue is empty. This is the mode for cron.

headingPath: On a Server You Control: Run It as a Daemon
chunks.text:
Keep the worker running with a process manager such as Supervisor, which restarts it whenever it stops. The limit options let it recycle itself regularly.

```ini
[program:rhapsody-queue]
command=php /var/www/app/rhapsody queue:work --queue=high,default --max-time=3600
directory=/var/www/app
autostart=true
autorestart=true
numprocs=2
process_name=%(program_name)s_%(process_num)02d
stopwaitsecs=70
```

Run as many workers as you like: each job is claimed by exactly one of them. `stopwaitsecs` gives a worker time to finish its current job when the process manager stops it.

headingPath: On Shared Hosting: Run It from Cron
chunks.text:
No process manager? Start a worker every minute. It processes whatever is waiting and exits.

```bash
* * * * * cd /path/to/app && php rhapsody queue:work --stop-when-empty --max-time=55 >> /dev/null 2>&1
```

If a run is still busy when the next one starts, that is fine: the two simply share the work.

A job that has used all its attempts, or whose stored data can no longer be read, is moved to the `failed_jobs` table together with the error and stack trace. Every failure is also written to `storage/logs/queue.log`.

```bash
php rhapsody queue:failed          # list them
php rhapsody queue:retry 12        # put one back on its queue
php rhapsody queue:retry all       # put them all back
php rhapsody queue:flush           # delete them all (asks first; --force skips the question)
```

A retried job starts again with a fresh attempt count.

Command | What it does
`queue:install [--migrate]` | Publishes the migration for the `jobs` and `failed_jobs` tables. Safe to run twice.
`queue:work` | Processes jobs. See the options above.
`queue:failed` | Lists failed jobs with their id, queue, time and error.
`queue:retry <id|all>` | Puts one failed job, or all of them, back on their queue.
`queue:flush [--force]` | Permanently deletes every failed job.

- A job may run more than once. If a worker dies after finishing the work but before the job is marked done, the job is handed out again. Write jobs so that running twice does no harm (check whether the email was already sent, use an upsert instead of an insert).
- Dispatch after you commit. Dispatch once the data the job needs is saved. A worker can pick the job up almost immediately, and it will not see changes that are still inside an open transaction.
- Keep `#[Timeout]` below the retry window. A reservation that is older than 90 seconds is treated as abandoned and the job is handed to another worker. The default job timeout is 60 seconds, which fits; if you raise it, raise the driver's `retryAfter` too (see below).
- Timeouts and a graceful stop need `pcntl`. On Linux and macOS the worker aborts a job that exceeds its timeout, and finishes its current job before exiting on `SIGTERM` or Ctrl+C. Windows (for example a local WAMP setup) has no `pcntl`: jobs run without a time limit, and stopping the worker mid-job leaves the job to be retried once its reservation expires.
- A crashing job cannot loop forever. Every time a job is picked up it counts as an attempt. A job that keeps killing its worker still ends up in the failed jobs once its attempts are used.
- Jobs are signed. Each job is stored with a signature made from your `APP_KEY`. A row that was altered, or inserted by hand, is rejected and moved to the failed jobs. If you rotate the key, list the old one in `APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS` so jobs already waiting can still be read.
- Renaming or deleting a job class makes waiting jobs of that class unreadable, and they go to the failed jobs. Let the queue drain first, or keep the old class until it has.
- Restart workers after a deploy. A running worker keeps the old code in memory. Stop it (a process manager will start a fresh one) or let `--max-time` recycle it. Cron workers pick up new code on their own.
- Queue order. Within a queue, jobs run oldest first. To make some work more urgent, give it its own queue and list that queue first: `--queue=high,default`.
- Works on every supported database. MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server and SQLite use the same tables and the same queries. The `priority` and `meta` columns are reserved for add-on modules and are not used by core.
- If the tables are missing, the worker and `dispatch()` stop with a message telling you to run `queue:install --migrate`.

Rhapsody's React integration gives you the best of both worlds: the power and interactivity of React components within your traditional Twig templates. Whether you want to embed a single interactive component ("React Islands") or build a full single-page application, the integration seamlessly bridges your PHP backend with a modern React + Vite frontend.

Key Benefits:

- ✅ React Islands – embed components directly in Twig templates
- ✅ Full SPA Support – render entire pages with React
- ✅ Vite HMR – instant hot module reloading during development
- ✅ XSS-Safe Props – JSON props embedded in safe script blocks
- ✅ CSRF Protection – automatic token injection for secure POST requests
- ✅ Production Manifest – fingerprinted assets with import preloading

The React integration is available as a core feature. To install it into your application, run:

```bash
php rhapsody react:install
```

This command scaffolds:

- `vite.config.js` – Vite build configuration
- `package.json` – npm manifest with React + Vite dependencies
- `resources/js/app.jsx` – JavaScript entry point (the Rhapsody bridge)
- `resources/js/components/Welcome.jsx` – example component
- Updates `.env` and `.env.example` with Vite configuration variables

Next Steps:

1. 1. Run `npm install` to install JavaScript dependencies
2. 2. Development: set `VITE_DEV_SERVER=true` in `.env` and run `npm run dev`
3. 3. Production: run `npm run build`
The React integration uses two environment variables that control how assets are loaded:

When set to `true`, assets are served from the Vite dev server running on `localhost:5173`. This enables Hot Module Replacement (HMR) for instant feedback during development.

```bash
VITE_DEV_SERVER=true
```

The port Vite runs on. Defaults to `5173`. Change this if you're running multiple Vite instances.

```bash
VITE_PORT=5173
```

Production Ready:

When `VITE_DEV_SERVER=false` or omitted, the integration automatically uses the production build from `{ROOT_DIRECTORY}/public/build/` with fingerprinted asset URLs from the Vite manifest.

Generate new React components quickly with the `make:react` command:

```bash
# Simple component
php rhapsody make:react Dashboard

# Nested component
php rhapsody make:react Users/ProfileCard

# Any level of nesting
php rhapsody make:react Admin/Settings/UserPreferences
```

Components are created in `resources/js/components/` with a preconfigured template. The component name must be PascalCase (e.g., `UserProfile`, `ActivityFeed`).

When `VITE_DEV_SERVER=true`, assets are served from the Vite dev server. This provides:

- Hot Module Replacement (HMR) – instant updates without page reload
- Fast build times – only what's needed is compiled
- Source maps for debugging

Run the dev server:

```bash
npm run dev
```

When `VITE_DEV_SERVER=false`, assets are built and served from the production manifest. This provides:

- Minified, optimized assets
- Fingerprinted filenames for cache busting
- Automatic preloading of imported modules
- CSS extraction and optimization

Build for production:

```bash
npm run build
```

1. Controller → $this->react() or $this->view()

└── BaseController renders the page with embedded props

└── ViteManifest resolves asset URLs

2. Browser loads the page

└── HTML contains mount point(s) and props

└── JavaScript loads the Rhapsody bridge

3. React renders the component

└── Full-page → single root mount

└── Islands → multiple independent mounts

Props are serialised with `JSON_HEX_TAG`, which escapes `</script>` sequences:

```php
$propsJson = json_encode($props, JSON_HEX_TAG | JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE);
```

This prevents `</script>` injection inside the JSON block, making it safe to embed arbitrary user data.
The integration automatically injects the CSRF token as a `<meta>` tag. Use it in your React components for secure POST requests as shown above.

1. Generate the component: `php rhapsody make:react Dashboard`
2. Edit `resources/js/components/Dashboard.jsx`
3. In a controller: `return $this->react('Dashboard', $props);`
4. Start Vite: `npm run dev`

Protect your application's sensitive forms (login, registration, password reset, etc.) from automated abuse. The Rhapsody framework provides a seamless integration with Google reCAPTCHA v2 (Checkbox) through a Twig view injector and a corresponding validation rule.

Prerequisite: You must have a valid Google reCAPTCHA API key pair. Register your site here. Choose "reCAPTCHA v2" and "I'm not a robot" Checkbox.

Store your site and secret keys inside the application's `.env` file. The framework reads these values via `$_ENV`.

```bash
RECAPTCHA_SITE_KEY="your_site_key_here"
RECAPTCHA_SECRET_KEY="your_secret_key_here"
```

Note: If either key is missing or empty, the widget will not render and the server‑side validation will automatically fail. This prevents insecure fallback behaviour.

The base controller (or a custom view composer) automatically binds the reCAPTCHA script and widget markup to the `captcha_form` variable. You only need to print this variable inside your Twig form.

Critical: Because the variable contains raw HTML, you must use the Twig `|raw` filter. Without it, the browser will display the markup as plain text and the widget will not work.

```twig
<form action="/register" method="POST">
<!-- CSRF Protection – always include for POST forms -->
{{ csrf_field() }}

    <label for="email">Email</label>
    <input type="email" name="email" id="email" required>

    <!-- The reCAPTCHA widget will be inserted here -->
    {{ captcha_form|raw }}

    <button type="submit">Register</button>
</form>
```

The rendered HTML includes:

- The Google API script ( `https://www.google.com/recaptcha/api.js`) loaded asynchronously.
- A `div` with class `g-recaptcha` and your site key as a `data-sitekey` attribute.

You can customise the widget by passing additional attributes (e.g., `data-theme`, `data-size`) by extending the `Recaptcha::render()` method – see the source code in `Rhapsody\Core\Helpers\Recaptcha`.

- Widget does not appear: Check that `RECAPTCHA_SITE_KEY` is set in your `.env` and that the variable is printed with `|raw`.
- Validation always fails: Ensure your secret key is correct and that the domain in your Google admin panel matches your application's domain (including subdomain and protocol).
- “Invalid input secret” error: The secret key may be mis‑typed or you may be using a different environment key than expected.
- Rate limiting or timeouts: Google’s API may occasionally be slow; the helper returns `false` on any network error. Consider logging these failures for monitoring.

The `Rhapsody\Core\Request` class provides an object-oriented way to interact with the current HTTP request. It encapsulates all the information about the request, such as GET and POST data, server variables, and uploaded files, making your application more secure and easier to work with.

An instance of the `Request` object is automatically created and passed as the first argument to every controller method by the router.

headingPath: Retrieving Input (GET, POST, JSON, PUT, etc.)
chunks.text:
The `getBody()` method intelligently handles all input sources:

- If the `Content-Type` is `application/json`, it decodes the JSON payload.
- For standard form submissions ( `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`), it returns `$_POST`.
- For `PUT`, `PATCH`, or `DELETE` requests with form data, it parses `php://input` automatically.

```php
$allInput = $request->getBody();
$email    = $allInput['email'] ?? null;
```

`string()`, `int()`, `bool()` and `array()` read a single input value and hand it back as exactly the type you asked for, so you don't need casts or `isset()` checks. They look in the request body first (form fields or a JSON payload, as described above) and then fall back to the query string.

```php
$name   = $request->string('name');        // '' when missing
$page   = $request->int('page', 1);        // 1 when missing or not an integer
$active = $request->bool('active');        // false when missing
$tags   = $request->array('tags');         // [] when missing or not an array
                                           // ?tags[]=php&tags[]=twig  gives  ['php', 'twig']
```

Method | Accepts | Gives the default when
`string($key, $default = '')` | Strings, ints, floats and bools (converted to a string) | The value is missing, `null`, or an array
`int($key, $default = 0)` | Ints and integer-like strings such as `'42'` or `'-7'` | The value is anything else, including `'1.5'`, `'12abc'`, an empty string, or a decimal number
`bool($key, $default = false)` | `true`/`false`, `1`/`0`, and the strings `true`, `false`, `on`, `off`, `yes`, `no` (case-insensitive) | The value is anything else. An empty string is read as `false`, not as the default
`array($key)` | Arrays, such as `tags[]=a&tags[]=b` or a JSON array | The value is missing or not an array (it always returns `[]`; there is no default argument)

A typical controller reads like this:

```php
public function showUsers(Request $request): Response
{
    $page       = $request->int('page', 1);
    $sort       = $request->string('sort', 'name');
    $subscribed = $request->bool('subscribed');   // an unchecked checkbox is never submitted, so this is false
    $roles      = $request->array('roles');

    // ...
}
```

headingPath: What the Accessors Do Not Do
chunks.text:
- They never throw. A bad or missing value quietly becomes the default. If a value is required, check it with the Validator and reject the request. (This is the opposite of the `Config` reader, which throws on a missing or wrongly-typed key. See Support Helpers.)
- They don't validate or sanitize. `int()` guarantees you receive an integer, not a sensible one, so clamp or range-check values like page numbers and limits yourself. `string()` returns the text exactly as it was sent, without the HTML-encoding that `getQueryParam()` applies, so escape it on output (Twig does this automatically) and never build SQL from it.
- They work on the Request's own data. Unlike `getQueryParam()`, which reads PHP's `$_GET` directly, these methods use the data the `Request` was built with. That makes them work with requests created by `Request::create()` in your tests (see Unit Testing).

The accessors above are built on `input()`, which returns a single raw value (body first, then the query string) or a default of your choosing. `all()` returns every input value at once: the query string and the request body merged, with body values winning when a key appears in both.

```php
$value = $request->input('q', 'none');   // raw value, any type
$data  = $request->all();                // query string + body
```

The `getCanonicalUrl()` method builds a clean, SEO‑friendly canonical URL for the current request. It automatically:

- Detects the correct protocol ( `http://` or `https://`).
- Uses the host from `$_SERVER['HTTP_HOST']`.
- Strips the path to its bare structure (no extra text).
- Retains only allowed query parameters (by default, only `page` is kept).

This method is used internally by the main layout to generate the `<link rel="canonical">` tag, but you can also call it manually if you need the value elsewhere.

```php
// Keep only 'page' and 'category' in the canonical URL
$canonical = $request->getCanonicalUrl(['page', 'category']);
```

If you need to access raw GET or POST values directly, you can use the `get()` and `post()` methods:

```php
$userId = $request->get('user_id');   // from $_GET
$email  = $request->post('email');    // from $_POST
```

All controller methods in Rhapsody must return an instance of the `Rhapsody\Core\Response` object (or a class that extends it, like `RedirectResponse`). This object represents the complete HTTP response that will be sent back to the browser, including the content, status code, and headers.
While you can create a `Response` object manually, it's usually more convenient to use the helper methods provided by the `BaseController`.
Rhapsody provides a `RedirectResponse` class for handling HTTP redirects. The easiest way to create one is with the global `redirect()` helper function.
