chunks.text:
The `send()` method is called automatically by the framework to output the response. You rarely need to call it yourself, but it’s available if you need to manually flush the response.

It sets the status code, sends all headers, and prints the content.

By default, Rhapsody boots fresh on every single request — the container is built, every service binding is registered, modules boot, and routes load, all from scratch, every time. This is what makes Rhapsody work correctly on ordinary shared hosting and modest VPS environments with zero configuration. It's also, unavoidably, work that gets thrown away and redone on the very next request.

`arout/rhapsody-roadrunner` is an optional package that runs your application inside a RoadRunner worker process — a long-lived PHP process that stays booted and handles many requests in a loop, instead of one request per process. The container, your service bindings, the Doctrine `EntityManager`, the Twig environment, and everything else built during boot are constructed once and reused across every request the worker serves.

This is opt-in, and it's not for everyone. Classic per-request Rhapsody is, and will remain, the default and the recommendation for shared hosting. Reach for this package specifically when you're deploying to your own VPS or container and want to eliminate per-request boot overhead under real load.

- PHP 8.4.1 or greater (same as core Rhapsody)
- Shell/process access to run a long-lived binary — this rules out most shared hosting, since you can't normally start and supervise a persistent process there. A VPS, dedicated server, or container platform is required.
- The `sockets` PHP extension

Check `ext-sockets` before you install. RoadRunner's PHP worker communicates with the RoadRunner binary over a socket connection, so this extension is a hard requirement, not an optional one. Run `php -m | grep sockets` to check. Most VPS and dedicated server environments ship it enabled by default, but some locked-down shared hosts and minimal container images disable it — and on many of those, you won't have the permissions to enable it yourself. If `composer require` fails with a message about `ext-sockets`, this is why, and it means this deployment path isn't available to you on that host.

```bash
composer require arout/rhapsody-roadrunner
```

This installs the `Rhapsody\RoadRunner\RoadRunnerKernel` class plus two template files you'll need at your project root — a worker entry point and a RoadRunner config file. Copy them out of the package:

```bash
cp vendor/arout/rhapsody-roadrunner/stubs/worker.php.stub ./worker.php
cp vendor/arout/rhapsody-roadrunner/stubs/.rr.yaml.stub ./.rr.yaml
```

Both are yours to edit once copied — they're a starting point, not a file the package manages for you. `worker.php` is your application's entry point under RoadRunner, the same role `index.php` plays under classic PHP. `.rr.yaml` configures the RoadRunner server itself: how many worker processes to run, and when to recycle them.

You'll also need the RoadRunner binary itself, which is a separate download (it's a compiled Go binary, not a PHP package):

```bash
./vendor/bin/rr get
```

```bash
./rr serve
```

This starts the RoadRunner server, which spawns and supervises your `worker.php` processes according to `.rr.yaml` and begins forwarding HTTP requests to them. There's no Apache or PHP-FPM involved on the request path — RoadRunner is the server.

You must restart your workers after every deploy. Because `worker.php` and everything it boots stays loaded in memory for the life of the process, a worker that was already running when you deployed new code is still serving the old code — PHP doesn't hot-reload class definitions in a long-running process. This is the single most common mistake when moving from classic per-request PHP to a persistent-worker model: a deploy that looks successful while workers keep quietly serving stale code until they happen to restart on their own.

Restart workers as the final step of every deploy:

```bash
./rr reset
```

Everything built during boot — the container and its service bindings, the Doctrine `EntityManager`, the Twig environment, the registered routes and middleware configuration, installed modules — is constructed once per worker process and reused across every request it serves. This is where the performance benefit comes from.

The parts of a request that genuinely are per-request — the `Request` and `Response` objects, PHP's session, and a short list of internal bookkeeping — are explicitly reset on every single request by `Kernel::resetState()`, before your route even matches:

- The container's dependency-resolution trace is cleared, so the debug toolbar reflects only the current request.
- The router's last-matched-route is cleared, so no request can ever observe a route matched by the one before it.
- If a `Database` connection was opened, it's pinged and transparently reconnected if the underlying connection was dropped while the worker was idle — this happens naturally between requests due to database server timeouts, and would otherwise surface as a confusing connection error on whichever request happens to run next.
- The Doctrine `EntityManager`'s identity map is cleared, so entities loaded by a previous request never leak into the current one's object graph. If Doctrine had permanently closed it — which it does after certain unrecoverable ORM exceptions — it's discarded and transparently rebuilt from scratch instead.
- SQL query logs collected for the debug toolbar are cleared, so the query panel shows only the current request's queries, not every query since the worker started.

`$_GET`, `$_POST`, `$_SERVER`, `$_COOKIE`, and `$_FILES` are also repopulated from the actual incoming request on every iteration by `RoadRunnerKernel`, since a long-running process doesn't get fresh superglobals the way a new PHP process does.

The framework itself handles the reset concerns above automatically. But this is a genuinely different execution model than classic PHP, and it has one implication for your own application code that's worth understanding before you deploy on it:

Any `static` property in your own classes is now a cross-request leak risk. Under classic PHP, a static property's lifetime is bounded by the request, because the whole process ends afterward — so it was always safe, even if it looked sloppy. Under a persistent worker, that same static property now lives for the life of the worker process, which means data from one visitor's request can silently become visible to the next visitor's request if you're not careful. Before deploying existing application code under RoadRunner, audit it for static properties that hold request-specific data (a static cache of "the current user," a static accumulator, anything set once and read later in the same request) and make sure they're either request-scoped some other way, or explicitly cleared.

Code-level reset hygiene reduces leaks, but it's not realistic to guarantee it catches everything — especially in third-party dependencies you don't control. RoadRunner's supervisor can recycle (gracefully restart) a worker after it's handled a fixed number of requests, or if its memory usage crosses a threshold, whichever comes first. This is standard practice for any persistent-PHP-worker deployment, RoadRunner or otherwise — treat it as a backstop alongside the reset behavior above, not a replacement for it:

```yaml
http:
  pool:
    num_workers: 4
    max_jobs: 1000
    supervisor:
      max_worker_memory: 128
```

This example recycles a worker after 1,000 requests, or if it exceeds 128MB of memory — whichever happens first.

The router is the heart of the Rhapsody framework. It maps incoming browser requests to specific controller methods, allowing you to create clean, human-readable URLs. All routes for your web application are defined in the `/routes/web.php` and `/routes/api.php` files.

Rhapsody supports named routes, allowing you to generate URLs dynamically without hardcoding paths. This is especially useful when your application is installed in a subdirectory. To assign a name to a route, chain the `name()` method: ```php Router::get('/profile/{id}', [ProfileController::class, 'show'])->name('profile.show'); ``` You can then generate URLs using the `route()` Twig function in your views: ```twig View Profile ``` The `route()` function accepts the route name as the first argument and an optional associative array of parameters to replace the placeholders. If you need the base URL (including subdirectory) prepended, the `route()` function automatically uses `$_ENV['APP_URL'] . $_ENV['APP_BASE_URL']`. You can also generate URLs from PHP using the static method `Router::generateUrl($name, $params)`.

You can attach middleware to routes to filter requests (e.g., authentication, CSRF protection). Middleware are resolved from the container and executed before the controller.

```php
Router::get('/dashboard', [DashboardController::class, 'index'])
    ->middleware('auth'); // only authenticated users
```

Middleware can be defined in the `config.php` file under the `middleware.map` key.

The router uses the service container to resolve controllers and their dependencies. Your controller classes can type‑hint any service, and the container will inject them automatically. The router also accepts a `ContainerInterface` instance, allowing you to swap the container implementation if needed.

For performance, the container can be configured to lazy‑load services (see the Performance documentation).

A single route can serve both a full page load and a JSON response for the same data — check `Request::wantsJson()` (true when the client sends `Accept: application/json`) inside the controller action and branch to `$this->json(...)` instead of `$this->view(...)`. No separate API route needed. See AJAX Pagination for a full example.

For optimal performance, you can cache your routes by running:

```bash
php rhapsody route:cache
```

This will cache your routes to a flat file in `/storage/cache/routes/routes.php`; saving you the overhead of processing your routing definitions on every request. There is only one thing to be aware of - any time you add a new route, you must clear the cache by either deleting the file manually, or running `php rhapsody route:clear`, and then recompiling the cache with `php rhapsody route:cache` again. If you do not regenerate the cache after adding a new route, you will hit a 404 error when you attempt to visit the new page.

Additional notes on routing:

- It is recommended to leave route caching off in your dev environment.
- The route cache will be cleared automatically when you update the framework, or when you clear the app cache: `php rhapsody cache:clear`

The debug toolbar includes a Services and Middleware panel that show which routes were matched, which middleware were executed, and which services were resolved during the request. This is invaluable for profiling and debugging.
Rhapsody includes built‑in support for social authentication via Google and Facebook. See the Social Authentication documentation for setup instructions and route examples.
Rhapsody is built with security in mind and includes several features to protect your application from common vulnerabilities.

Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attacks trick users into performing unwanted actions. Rhapsody makes protection easy.

The `VerifyCsrfTokenMiddleware` runs globally on every request. It automatically validates CSRF tokens for all `POST` requests (and other “unsafe” methods like `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`). If the token is missing or invalid, the request is aborted with a 419 Page Expired error.

headingPath: Adding the CSRF Token to Forms
chunks.text:
Include the `csrf_field()` Twig function inside every form that submits with `method="POST"` (or uses a spoofed method). This generates a hidden input containing the user’s unique token.

```twig
<form action="/profile/update" method="POST">
    
    <!-- other fields -->
    <button type="submit">Update Profile</button>
</form>
```

For JSON requests, include the token in the request body under the key `_token`. The middleware intelligently looks for the token in both `$_POST` and the parsed JSON payload.

```json
{
    "_token": "generated_token_here",
    "name": "John Doe"
}
```
The `VerifyCsrfTokenMiddleware` is included in the `global` array in `config/middleware.php`. It runs automatically on every matched request. You can add your own global middleware there as well.
You can exclude certain URIs (e.g., webhooks) by editing the `$except` array in `app/Middleware/VerifyCsrfTokenMiddleware.php`. Wildcards (`*`) are supported.

The framework uses PHP's native `password_hash()` and `password_verify()` for all user authentication. Passwords are never stored in plain text and are protected with a modern, secure hashing algorithm. See `app/Models/User.php` and `app/Controllers/AuthController.php` for implementation details.
Rhapsody provides a set of tools to help you optimise your application for search engines and social media sharing.

The main layout automatically generates a `<link rel="canonical">` tag for every page. This tells search engines the preferred URL for your content, preventing duplicate content issues. The generation is handled by the `Request::getCanonicalUrl()` method, which you can customise by passing allowed query parameters.

Make sure the `APP_URL` variable is set correctly in your `.env` file.
The `Rhapsody\Core\SEO\SchemaOrg` class allows you to add JSON‑LD structured data to your pages. This helps search engines understand your content and can improve your appearance in rich results.

The `Rhapsody\Core\SEO\Sluggify` class provides a static method `transform()` that converts any string into a clean, SEO‑friendly URL slug. It handles accents, special characters, ampersands, and more.

The framework can automatically generate a `sitemap.xml` file for you. Simply navigate to `/sitemap.xml`. This file lists all your public pages, making it easy for search engines like Google to discover and index your entire site. You can customize which pages are included by editing `app/Controllers/SitemapController.php`.
A basic `robots.txt` file is included in the project root. You can edit this file to provide instructions to search engine crawlers, such as which pages or directories to disallow.

`Rhapsody\Core\Session` is a small static wrapper around PHP's native sessions. It gives you one consistent place to store per-visitor data (the logged-in user, one-time flash messages, the CSRF token) with secure cookie settings applied for you. There is nothing to instantiate: every method is static.

```php
use Rhapsody\Core\Session;

Session::set('cart_id', 42);

$cartId = Session::get('cart_id');          // 42
$theme  = Session::get('theme', 'light');   // 'light' (the default) when the key is not set
```

Start it once per request: `Session::start()` must have run before you read or write session data, and it must run only once per request. See Flash Messages for why a second call causes trouble.

Method | What it does
`Session::set($key, $value)` | Stores a value under a key.
`Session::get($key, $default = null)` | Returns the stored value, or `$default` when the key is not set.
`Session::has($key)` | Returns `true` if the key is set and its value is not `null`.
`Session::pull($key, $default = null)` | Returns the value and removes it in one step. Returns `$default` if the key was not set.
`Session::remove($key)` | Deletes a key.

`has()` treats a `null` value as “not set”. If you need to store a deliberate `null` and tell it apart from a missing key, store a different marker value instead.

headingPath: How long a flash message lives
chunks.text:
1. The message is available for the rest of the request that created it.
2. It stays available for the next request.
3. At the start of the request after that, `Session::start()` deletes it.

Reading a message with `getFlash()` removes it straight away, so read it once and keep the result in a variable if you need it more than once on the same page.

Danger: The aging of flash messages happens inside `Session::start()`. Calling it a second time in the same request ages the messages again and discards them before your page can show them.

Flash messages are stored under the key you give them, in the same namespace as values saved with `set()`. Choose flash keys (`success`, `error`, `status`) that you don't also use for ordinary session data.

`destroy()` does all three things needed to end a session properly. Doing only one or two leaves a usable session behind:

1. Empties `$_SESSION` immediately, so the data is gone for the remainder of the request.
2. Expires the session cookie in the visitor's browser.
3. Destroys the session on the server.

```php
Session::destroy();
```

`Session::start()` configures the session cookie before PHP starts the session:

- Lifetime: `0`, so the cookie lasts until the browser is closed.
- Path: `/`, so the session works across your whole site.
- HttpOnly: always on, so JavaScript cannot read the session ID.
- SameSite: `Lax`, which blocks the cookie on most cross-site POST requests.
- Secure: turned on automatically when the request is served over HTTPS, including behind a proxy that sends `X-Forwarded-Proto: https`.

If a session is already active, `start()` skips starting a new one, but it still ages the flash messages, which is why it must only run once per request.

The session uses three keys internally. Don't write to them yourself:

- `_token` – the CSRF token.
- `_flash_new` and `_flash_old` – the bookkeeping that tracks which flash messages to delete.

Every request your application handles in development mode (`APP_ENV=development`) can be saved as a single, redacted JSON file: the request, the matched route, the response status, every database query, timings, the last log lines and – if the request failed – the exception and its trace. It is the same data the Debug Toolbar shows, in a form you can keep, diff, attach to a bug report or hand to a tool.

💡 Tip: Snapshots are on by default in development and do nothing in production. There is nothing to install or call – make a request, then open the newest file in `storage/debug/snapshots`.

Snapshots are written for every response, not just successful HTML pages. That includes JSON API errors, redirects, 404s and requests that ended in an uncaught exception (those are captured by the error handler, because the normal end-of-request step never runs for them).

Section | Contents
`framework` | App version, environment, PHP version, SAPI, OS family
`request` | Method, URL, IP, headers, query string, body (size-limited), route middleware
`route` | Matched path, controller and action (or `null` if nothing matched)
`response` | HTTP status code
`performance` | Execution time (ms) and memory (MB)
`queries` | Total count, the first N queries (SQL, parameters, time, caller) and a summary of repeated query shapes
`cache`, `middleware`, `services` | Cache hit/miss stats, middleware timings, and the 25 slowest container resolutions
`session` | The session's keys and value types – never the values
`environment` | An allowlist of safe variables only (see below)
`logs` | The last lines of the PHP and web server logs, if readable
`exception` | `null`, or the class, message, location, a 15-frame trace and up to 3 previous exceptions

Files go to `storage/debug/snapshots/`, one per request, named by a sortable id (`YYYYmmdd-His-microseconds-xxxx.json`) so the newest file is always last alphabetically. Only the newest 25 are kept – older files are deleted as new ones arrive, so the folder never grows without bound.

- Writes are atomic (temp file, then rename), so you never read a half-written snapshot.
- The folder gets a deny-all `.htaccess` and an empty `index.html` the first time it is created, in case your web root ever includes `storage/`.
- Add `/storage/debug` to `.gitignore` (new skeletons already do).

Everything is optional. Add a `debug.snapshots` section to `config/config.php` to change the defaults:

```php
'debug' => [
    'snapshots' => [
        'enabled'         => Env::bool('DEBUG_SNAPSHOTS', true),
        'keep'            => Env::int('DEBUG_SNAPSHOTS_KEEP', 25),
        'max_body_bytes'  => 8192,
        'max_queries'     => 100,
        'log_lines'       => 20,
        'redact_keys'     => [],
        'env_allowlist'   => [],
        'ignore_prefixes' => ['/img/'],
    ],
],
```

Option | Default | Meaning
`enabled` | `true` | Turn recording off without touching `APP_ENV` (`DEBUG_SNAPSHOTS=false`)
`keep` | `25` | How many snapshot files to keep
`max_body_bytes` | `8192` | Request bodies longer than this are cut off (`truncated: true`)
`max_queries` | `100` | Individual queries listed; the true total is still reported
`log_lines` | `20` | Log lines included from each log
`redact_keys` | `[]` | Extra key names to mask, e.g. `['ssn', 'iban']`
`env_allowlist` | `[]` | Extra environment variable names to include
`ignore_prefixes` | `['/img/']` | Requests whose path contains any of these are not recorded (keeps image requests from pushing out useful snapshots). Paths under `/_rhapsody/` (the framework's own development endpoints, such as the AI helpers) are always skipped
A snapshot is meant to be shared, so secrets are removed while it is built – an unredacted version never exists on disk. The `Redactor` works in two layers:

Any header, query parameter, form or JSON field, or route parameter whose name looks sensitive has its whole value replaced with `[REDACTED]`. Names are compared ignoring case and separators, so `X-Api-Key`, `api_key` and `apiKey` all match. Built in: `password`, `secret`, `token`, `apikey`, `authorization`, `cookie`, `credential`, `private`, `signature`, `csrf`, `bearer`, `jwt`, `salt`, `hash`, `phpsessid`, plus the whole words `pass`, `pwd`, `key`, `auth`, `sig` and `sid`. JSON bodies are redacted field by field, at any depth.

Free text – bodies, SQL, log lines, exception messages, URLs – is scrubbed for things that look like secrets wherever they appear:

- `Bearer …` and `Basic …` credentials, and JSON Web Tokens
- Credentials inside URLs ( `mysql://user:pass@host`)
- Stripe, Google, AWS and GitHub key formats
- `Cookie:` / `Set-Cookie:` lines
- `password=…`, `"token": "…"` and similar key/value pairs

- SQL parameters have no names, so they are masked as a whole whenever the statement mentions a sensitive column or table (for example `UPDATE users SET password = ?`).
- Session data keeps its shape but every value becomes its type, e.g. `[REDACTED int]`.
- Environment variables are never dumped wholesale. Only an allowlist is included ( `APP_ENV`, `DB_HOST`, `DB_NAME`, `CACHE_DRIVER` and a few others); add your own with `env_allowlist`.

⚠️ Redaction is best effort: Pattern matching cannot recognise every secret. A field called `note` that happens to hold a password will not be caught. Skim a snapshot before posting it publicly, and add your own field names to `redact_keys`.

Queries are grouped by shape: literals are replaced by `?`, `IN (…)` lists are collapsed and whitespace is normalised, so `WHERE id = 7` and `WHERE id = 912` count as the same query. A shape that runs more than three times in one request is flagged. The `queries.n_plus_one` section lists each flagged shape with its count, total time, an example and up to three callers, so you can see where the loop is. The Debug Toolbar's database tab uses the same logic, so both always agree.

- Development only. Nothing is recorded or written when `APP_ENV` is anything but `development`.
- Recording can never break a request: if the disk is full or the folder is not writable, the snapshot is silently skipped.
- The snapshot is built from the Debug Toolbar's collected data, so it has the same blind spots (for example, response bodies are not stored).
- Long-running RoadRunner workers have not been verified with snapshots yet; use the standard front controller when you need them.
Rhapsody provides a built‑in `SocialAuthController` that handles authentication through Google and Facebook using the `league/oauth2-client` packages.

The required packages are already included in the core if you installed via Composer. If you're upgrading, run:

```bash
composer require league/oauth2-client league/oauth2-google league/oauth2-facebook
```

Add the following environment variables to your `.env` file:

```env

GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET=your_google_client_secret

FACEBOOK_REDIRECT_URI=http://localhost/rhapsody-dev/auth/callback/facebook
```

The redirect URIs must match exactly what you have registered in the Google and Facebook developer consoles.
In your login view, you can generate the provider links using the named route: ```twig Login with Google Login with Facebook ```
The controller uses `App\Models\User` by default. If you're using a different model, you can override the `handleProviderCallback` method or extend the controller.

To add other providers (e.g., GitHub, Twitter), you'll need to install their respective OAuth2 packages, add a new case to the `getProvider()` method in `SocialAuthController`, and update your routes accordingly.

Class | Use it for | When something is wrong
`Config` | Reading values from the application config array, with dot notation and type checks | Throws `RuntimeException`
`Env` | Reading values from your `.env` file / the environment | Never throws; returns your default
`Fs` | Reading, writing and locating files | Throws `RuntimeException`
`Json` | Encoding and decoding JSON | Throws `JsonException`

Why exceptions? PHP's own functions report failure by returning `false` (or `null`), which is easy to ignore and then shows up three calls later as a confusing error. These helpers fail loudly where the problem is, and always return the type their name promises. `Env` is the one deliberate exception, because an unset environment variable is normal and a default is the natural answer.

Method | Returns
`all()` | The entire config array
`has($key)` | `true` if the key exists. A key set to `null` still counts as existing.
`get($key, $default = null)` | The raw value, or `$default` if the key does not exist
`string($key, ?string $default = null)` | A `string`
`int($key, ?int $default = null)` | An `int`
`bool($key, ?bool $default = null)` | A `bool`
`array($key, ?array $default = null)` | An `array`

Reach into nested arrays with dots. An exact key match is tried first, so a key that literally contains a dot still works.

```php
// config/config.php
return [
    'mail' => [
        'host' => 'smtp.example.com',
        'port' => '587',
    ],
];
```

```php
$config->string('mail.host');       // 'smtp.example.com'
$config->int('mail.port');          // 587 (the string '587' is converted)
$config->int('mail.timeout', 30);   // 30  (key missing, so the default is used)
$config->array('mail');             // ['host' => '...', 'port' => '587']
```

The key names above are just an example; use whatever your own `config.php` defines.

- Missing key or `null` value: the default is returned if you passed one. Otherwise a `RuntimeException` is thrown: `Missing config key 'mail.username'.`
- Wrong type: a `RuntimeException` is thrown that names the key and what it actually was, e.g. `Config key 'mail.port' must be int, array given.`
- .env-friendly conversion: values that arrive as strings are converted when the conversion is unambiguous.
  - `string()` accepts strings, ints and floats.
  - `int()` accepts ints and integer-looking strings such as `'587'` (but not `'5.5'`).
  - `bool()` accepts booleans, plus strings or ints that read as a boolean: `true`/ `false`, `1`/ `0`, `on`/ `off`, `yes`/ `no`.
  - `array()` accepts arrays only.

`Rhapsody\Core\Support\Env` gives typed access to environment values, such as those loaded from your `.env` file. It looks in `$_ENV` first and then falls back to `getenv()`. All methods are static.

Method | Returns
`Env::get($key)` | The raw value as a `string`, or `null` if the variable is not set
`Env::string($key, $default = '')` | The value, or `$default` when unset
`Env::int($key, $default = 0)` | The value as an `int`, or `$default` when unset or not numeric
`Env::bool($key, $default = false)` | The value as a `bool`, or `$default` when unset or not recognised

```php
$url      = Env::string('APP_URL');
$theme    = Env::string('APP_THEME', 'default');
$retries  = Env::int('QUEUE_RETRIES', 3);        // example variable
$maintain = Env::bool('MAINTENANCE_MODE', false);  // example variable
```

For `Env::bool()`, `true`, `1`, `yes` and `on` are true, and `false`, `0`, `no`, `off` and an empty value are false (any case). Anything else returns your default.

`Env` never throws. If a variable must be set, check for `null` yourself:

```php
$apiKey = Env::get('PAYMENT_API_KEY')
    ?? throw new RuntimeException('PAYMENT_API_KEY is not set in .env');
```

`Env` reads the raw environment. `Config` reads your application's config array, which is usually itself built from environment values. In application code, prefer `Config` so each setting is read from one place; reach for `Env` in the config file itself and in early boot code that runs before the config exists.

- All four classes are `final`. If you want a project-specific variation, wrap them in your own small class rather than extending them.
- `Env`, `Fs` and `Json` are static; there is nothing to instantiate or inject. `Config` is an object, so it is injected.
- The Request object offers the same style of typed access for request input.

chunks.pageTitle: Using Tailwind CSS in a Theme
chunks.text:
Rhapsody is CSS-agnostic: it doesn't ship a Tailwind build step and it doesn't care how your stylesheet is produced. A Tailwind theme is simply a regular theme whose stylesheet happens to be compiled by you and linked from your layout. This page walks through the full workflow, from installing Tailwind to activating the theme.

The short version: create the theme folder, compile Tailwind into `public/themes/<theme_name>/css/`, link that file from your `main.twig`, and set `APP_THEME` in `.env`. Tailwind runs at build time only, so nothing about it executes on the server.

chunks.pageTitle: Using Tailwind CSS in a Theme
chunks.text:
1. Create the theme folder and a `main.twig` layout.
2. Install Tailwind (Node is only needed on your development machine).
3. Create an `input.css` that tells Tailwind where your templates live.
4. Build the CSS into the theme's public folder.
5. Link the compiled file from the `styles` block of `main.twig`.
6. Activate the theme with `APP_THEME`.

chunks.pageTitle: Using Tailwind CSS in a Theme
chunks.text:
Every theme lives in its own folder under `views/themes/`. The layout must be named `main.twig` and sit in a `layouts` subfolder:

```bash
views/themes/my_theme/
├── layouts/
│   └── main.twig
├── auth/           ← login, register, forgot/reset password overrides
├── errors/         ← 404.twig, 500.twig, ...
└── pages/          ← your page templates

public/themes/my_theme/
└── css/
    └── my_theme.css   ← compiled Tailwind output (generated, see below)
```

See Creating custom themes for how view resolution and overrides work.

chunks.pageTitle: Using Tailwind CSS in a Theme
chunks.text:
From your application root (the folder containing `views/` and `public/`):

```bash
npm init -y
npm install -D tailwindcss @tailwindcss/cli
```

Optionally add the typography plugin if you render long-form content with the `prose` classes:

```bash
npm install -D @tailwindcss/typography
```

These commands target Tailwind v4. If you are on v3, see Tailwind v3 below.

chunks.pageTitle: Using Tailwind CSS in a Theme
Using Tailwind CSS in a Theme
chunks.text:
Compile into your theme's public folder. Add these as scripts in `package.json` so you don't have to remember them:

```json
{
    "scripts": {
        "css:watch": "tailwindcss -i ./input.css -o ./public/themes/my_theme/css/my_theme.css --watch",
        "css:build": "tailwindcss -i ./input.css -o ./public/themes/my_theme/css/my_theme.css --minify"
    }
}
```

```bash
# While developing: rebuilds on every template change
npm run css:watch

# Before deploying or releasing: minified output
npm run css:build
```

You can also run the CLI directly with `npx @tailwindcss/cli -i ./input.css -o ./public/themes/my_theme/css/my_theme.css`.

Rebuild whenever you add or change classes in a template. A page that looks right in one place and unstyled in another almost always means the build is stale or the template isn't covered by an `@source` path.

chunks.pageTitle: Using Tailwind CSS in a Theme
Using Tailwind CSS in a Theme
chunks.text:
- Build asset URLs with `{{ base_url }}` rather than hard-coded paths, so your theme keeps working when the app is installed in a subdirectory.
- The `scripts` block must keep the `vite_assets()` and `schema_markup|raw` lines exactly as shown. Any child template that overrides `scripts` must call `{{ parent() }}`.
- The framework's default layout already emits the canonical link tag from `Request::getCanonicalUrl()`. A custom layout that replaces it should emit it once, since duplicates hurt SEO.
- If your JavaScript sends `fetch()` POST requests, add a `<meta name="csrf-token" content="{{ csrf_token() }}">` tag in `head_extensions` and send the value as `_token` in the request body. The CSRF middleware doesn't read headers.

chunks.pageTitle: Using Tailwind CSS in a Theme
chunks.text:
Set the theme name in `.env`. The value must match the folder name under `views/themes/` exactly:

```bash
APP_THEME=my_theme
```

Styling doesn't change the framework's form requirements. Every form in your theme still needs the CSRF field and, where reCAPTCHA is used, the captcha tag:

```twig
<form method="post" action="{{ base_url }}/contact">
    {{ csrf_field() }}
    <input name="email" type="email"
           class="w-full rounded-lg border border-gray-300 px-3 py-2
                  dark:border-gray-700 dark:bg-gray-900">
    {{ captcha_form|raw }}
    {% include 'partials/button.twig' with { label: 'Send', type: 'submit' } %}
</form>
```

Controllers that process the form should validate with the framework's Validation class and display any errors in the template.

chunks.pageTitle: Using Tailwind CSS in a Theme
chunks.text:
- Ship minified CSS. Use `--minify` for anything you deploy.
- Don't use the Tailwind Play CDN script in production. It compiles in the browser and is intended for prototyping only.
- Keep `@source` narrow. Scan your theme folder rather than the whole project.
- Self-host fonts and reference them from `@theme` or `@font-face` rules in `input.css`.
- Ship the compiled file with the theme. People installing your theme shouldn't need Node just to get working styles. Include the unminified source and `input.css` if you want them to be able to recompile.

chunks.pageTitle: Using Tailwind CSS in a Theme
chunks.text:
If you plan to submit your theme to the Marketplace, the usual theme rules apply on top of the above:

- `main.twig` lives in `views/themes/<theme_name>/layouts` and contains all the required blocks in their documented formats.
- Auth views belong in `views/themes/<theme_name>/auth` and error pages in `views/themes/<theme_name>/errors`.
- Every form includes `csrf_field()` and `captcha_form|raw`.
- The theme must not create new folders in the application root. Keep any Tailwind source files inside the theme's own folders.
- Compiled CSS must be included, since reviewers and users won't run your build.

chunks.text:
- The page has no styling at all. Open the browser's network tab and check the CSS request. A 404 usually means a wrong path, or an `.htaccess` rule that doesn't allow `public/themes/...` (patterns anchored with `^/public/` can break when the app lives in a subdirectory).
- Some classes work, others don't. The build is stale, or the template isn't covered by an `@source` path, or the class name is being built dynamically.
- My CSS loads, but I still see the default theme's pages. Check that `APP_THEME` matches the folder name exactly, and that you're editing files under `views/themes/<theme_name>/` rather than a top-level copy. Clear the cache if you have view caching enabled.
- Built-in pages (auth, errors) look unstyled. Either override them in your theme or add the core views to `@source`.
- The page flashes light before switching to dark. The inline theme script must run in `<head>`, before the stylesheet and body render.
- `dark:` classes do nothing. You're using the class strategy but the `@custom-variant` line (v4) or `darkMode: 'class'` (v3) is missing, or the `dark` class isn't being set on `<html>`.

Rhapsody ships with a ready‑to‑run testing environment built on PHPUnit. You get a robust base `TestCase` class that integrates with the framework's container, HTTP routing, and Doctrine ORM, plus convenient traits and mocks to speed up your feature and unit tests.

Quick Start: Run `./vendor/bin/phpunit` from the project root. All tests are located in the `tests/` directory.
All your test classes should extend `Rhapsody\Core\Testing\TestCase`. This base class automatically boots a fresh application container in `setUp()`, so you have access to all registered services.

- Test coverage: Use `phpunit --coverage-html coverage/` to generate an HTML coverage report (requires Xdebug or pcov).
- Parallel testing: For large suites, consider using `paratest` or PHPUnit's process isolation.
- Environment separation: Create a separate `.env.testing` file for test‑specific settings (e.g., database credentials, mail drivers).
- Custom assertions: Extend `TestResponse` to add your own helpers for domain‑specific responses.

- Container not refreshed: Each test method runs in a fresh container. Do not rely on global state between tests.
- Database not rebuilt: Always call `setUpDatabase()` if using `RefreshesDatabase`. You can also call it in `setUp()` or in a `@before` annotation.
- Mocking final classes: PHPUnit cannot mock final classes; use `swap()` with a custom implementation instead.
- Response content missing: Ensure the router actually returns a response; if a controller throws an exception, the test will fail early.

For further details, refer to the official PHPUnit documentation and the framework's source code in `Rhapsody\Core\Testing`.
Understand the separation between Rhapsody's core views and your application's custom themes. Learn how to safely override, extend, or completely replace the default design system.

Rhapsody makes it easy to create custom themes or override the default design. All theme files live in the project’s `/views/themes/` directory – not inside `/app/views/` or the core package.

The framework uses Tailwind CSS v4.3 for the default design. If you extend the core theme, you inherit these styles automatically.

The active theme is determined by the `APP_THEME` environment variable in your `.env` file.

```bash
APP_THEME=my_custom_theme
```

If `APP_THEME` is not set, the framework falls back to the `default` theme.

The themes directory is located at:

```bash
/views/themes/
├── default/               ← fallback theme (always present)
│   ├── layouts/
│   │   └── main.twig
│   │   └── navbar.twig
│   ├── home/
│   └── errors/
├── my_custom_theme/       ← your active theme
│   ├── layouts/
│   │   └── main.twig      ← custom layout (optional)
│   │   └── navbar.twig
│   ├── home/
│   └── errors/
└── ...
```

The framework core ships with only a small set of views:

- Documentation pages ( `@core/docs/...`)
- Authentication pages (login, register) – accessible as `auth/login.twig`, etc.
- Error pages (404, 500) – accessible as `errors/404.twig`

These are available as a fallback only for those specific pages. If you render any other view (e.g., `home/index.twig`) and it does not exist in your active theme or the default theme, the framework will not look in the core for it. Instead, Twig will throw a `LoaderError`.

You are responsible for providing all the views your application needs – either in your active theme or the default theme. The core is not a complete view library.

To override any of the core‑provided views (login, register, error pages, etc.), simply create a file with the same relative path inside your active theme.

For example, to override the default 404 error page, create:

```bash
/views/themes/my_custom_theme/errors/404.twig
```

The framework will use your version instead of the core one. You don’t need to use `@core` when overriding – the loader checks your theme first.

The search order for any template is:

1. Active theme – `/views/themes//`
2. Default theme – `/views/themes/default/`
3. Core views – only for the specific pages listed above (via `@core` namespace or fallback)

Naturally, you'll want to create your own navigation menu. To do so, you will need to create a

navbar.twig

view file inside `/layouts` in your template directory: `/views/themes/{theme-name}/layouts/`. If you plan on reusing the core styles, it would be a good idea to view the core navbar to see its structure / styles.

/vendor/arout/rhapsody-core/resources/views/themes/default/layouts/navbar.twig

Or even better, simply copy it to your theme directory and modify it there.

Note: it may be necessary to copy over core's `main.twig` as well, and adjust the location of the navigation block, if you want your navbar on the bottom of the screen, or other conditions where the default location may interfere with your layout.

headingPath: Creating a Completely Custom Theme (From Scratch)
chunks.text:
If you want a totally custom design that does not rely on the framework's default styles or layout, you can build your own parent template.

- Do not use `@core` in your templates.
- Create your own `layouts/main.twig` inside your theme.
- Include your own CSS (e.g., via `<link>` tags, or use your own build tool).
- You are responsible for providing the necessary global Twig variables (like `base_url`, `auth`, `flash`) if you need them – they are still available globally, but you must output them as needed.

headingPath: Creating a Completely Custom Theme (From Scratch)
Every theme must define the same blocks as the default theme
chunks.text:
Twig's behavior when a child template overrides a block that doesn't exist anywhere in the layout it extends is to silently drop that content — no error, no warning, just missing output. For a block as foundational as `content` or `scripts`, that's a uniquely confusing way to fail: the page renders successfully, just without whatever a page template put in that block.

To catch this before it ever reaches that point, any theme other than `default` has its `layouts/main.twig` checked at boot for these exact block names — the same ones `views/themes/default/layouts/main.twig` itself defines:

```text
title, description, styles, head_extensions, body_class,
navigation, full_width_content, main, content, scripts
```

If any are missing, the application throws a fatal error at boot listing exactly which ones — not a blank page, not silently-missing content on whichever page happens to use that block first. A block is allowed to be empty (`{% block scripts %}{% endblock %}` is completely valid and satisfies the check), it just has to exist.

chunks.text:
The symptom is exactly as confusing as it sounds: everything works — the page loads, other pages using the same layout work fine — except one specific feature (a React-powered widget, a piece of interactive JS from the layout) is simply absent on this one page and nowhere else, with no error anywhere to point at why. If a page seems to be "missing" something that other pages on the same theme have, checking whether that page overrides a block without calling `parent()` first is the first thing worth checking.

The rule of thumb: if you're overriding a block that the layout you're extending puts anything into — not just scripts, this applies equally to `styles`, `head_extensions`, `navigation`, or any other block — call `parent()` as the first line of your override unless you specifically intend to replace that content entirely.

If you have reusable template components (e.g., from a module), you can add custom Twig namespaces in `bootstrap.php`:

```php
$loader->addPath('/path/to/module/views', 'module');
```

Then render: `$this->view('@module/index.twig')`.

- Extend core → use `@core` and override blocks (inherits Tailwind design).
- Override a core template → place a file with the same path in your active theme (for login, register, errors).
- Build a custom theme from scratch → create your own `layouts/main.twig` and avoid `@core`.
- Every non-default theme's `layouts/main.twig` must define all 10 required blocks (empty is fine) — checked at boot, with a fatal error listing exactly what's missing if it doesn't.
- Call `parent()` when overriding a block the layout already puts something into (scripts, styles, head_extensions, navigation) — otherwise that content is silently dropped on whichever page overrides it, including things like the React bridge's `vite_assets()` call.
- All theme files live in `/views/themes/`.
- The core design is built with Tailwind CSS v4.3.
- Core views are limited – only documentation, auth, and errors. For all other views, you must provide them yourself.

Rhapsody includes a powerful, non‑intrusive debug toolbar that appears at the bottom of every page when the application is in development mode (`APP_ENV=development`). It gives you real‑time insight into your application's performance, database queries, session data, middleware execution, dependency resolution, and more – all without cluttering your design.

💡 Tip: The toolbar is only injected into HTML responses. JSON/API responses are never altered.

The toolbar is divided into clickable tabs, each displaying a specific category of debug information. It also includes a persistent header that shows key metrics at a glance.

Rhapsody v1.0 Request 200 Logs Database 12 Queries Session Cache Performance Environment Time: 231 ms 45%

- Request Status – HTTP status code of the response (green = 200, red = 4xx/5xx).
- Execution Time – total time taken to process the request (in milliseconds).
- Memory Peak – a visual bar showing peak memory usage relative to the `memory_limit`; colour‑coded: green (safe), amber (warning), red (critical).
The Request tab provides a comprehensive snapshot of the incoming HTTP request. It's your go‑to for debugging routing issues, inspecting headers, or reproducing a request via cURL.

At the top, you'll find essential request metadata:

- Method – HTTP verb (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, etc.)
- Full URL – the complete URL of the request (including protocol, host, and query string)
- Client IP – the IP address of the client making the request
- Timestamp – exact time the request was received

Displays information about the matched route:

- Path – the URI path (after stripping `APP_BASE_URL`)
- Controller – the class handling the request
- Action – the method being called
- Parameters – dynamic route parameters (e.g., `user_id` from `/users/{user_id}`)
- Middleware – the list of route‑specific middleware (shown as a chain, e.g., `auth → guest`)

If no route matched, the panel shows a helpful "No route matched" message – ideal for debugging 404s.

All HTTP headers sent by the client are displayed in a clean key‑value table. This includes standard headers like `User-Agent`, `Accept`, `Content-Type`, and any custom headers your application or client may send.

If the request URL contains a query string (e.g., `/users?page=2&limit=10`), the parameters are displayed in a key‑value table. This is useful for debugging pagination, filters, or other GET parameters.

For POST, PUT, PATCH, or DELETE requests, the raw request body is displayed:

- If the body is valid JSON, it is automatically pretty‑printed for readability.
- If the body is plain text (e.g., form data), it is shown as‑is.
- If the request had no body, this section is omitted.

At the bottom of the Request tab, there is a 📋 Copy cURL button. Clicking it generates a complete `curl` command that replicates the current request – including method, URL, headers, and body. This is invaluable for:

- Reproducing bugs in a terminal
- Sharing a request with a colleague for debugging
- Testing API endpoints independently

Pro Tip: On Windows, use `curl.exe` instead of `curl` to avoid PowerShell's alias. The command generated in the toolbar will automatically use `curl.exe` on Windows.

🔒 Secrets are masked: `Authorization` and `Cookie` headers, tokens and password fields are replaced with `[REDACTED]` in the Request tab and in the copied command. Replace them by hand if you need to replay an authenticated request. See Request Snapshots for the full redaction rules.

**Why use cURL instead of just viewing page source?**

You might wonder: "I can already see the page source in my browser – why do I need a cURL command?" Here's why it's much more powerful:

**🔁 Reproduce anywhere**

Run the exact same request on any machine – your local terminal, a server, or a colleague's laptop. No browser, no cookies, no extensions.

**✏️ Modify and test**

Tweak headers, change parameters, or alter the request body to test different scenarios quickly. No need to navigate through forms or click around.

**📦 See the full response**

Page source only shows the HTML body. cURL shows everything – status code, headers, cookies, and timing details. Perfect for debugging APIs.

**📤 Share with teammates**

Instead of saying "click this button and fill out that form", you can share a one‑line command that reproduces the bug exactly.

**⏱️ Measure performance**

Add timing flags to measure DNS lookup, connection time, and total response time – metrics you can't get from page source.

**🤖 Automate testing**

Use the cURL command in CI/CD pipelines, load‑testing scripts, or monitoring tools to verify your endpoints automatically.

🧠 In a nutshell: View Page Source = quick visual inspection of the HTML structure. cURL Command = a complete, reproducible snapshot of the entire HTTP transaction.

Shows the last 50 lines of your PHP error log and Apache error log (or web server log). The log file paths are defined in `config.php` under the `logging` key.

Note: If a log file is not found or not readable, the toolbar will show a message indicating that.

Lists every SQL query executed during the request, along with:

- SQL – the raw query string
- Parameters – bound values (as JSON)
- Execution Time – time taken (in milliseconds)
- Caller – the file and line where the query was initiated

The toolbar automatically flags potential N+1 query patterns. This happens when the same query structure (after normalising literal values) is executed more than 3 times in a single request.

- If detected, a warning box appears at the top of the Database tab.
- Each flagged query is marked with a warning icon ( `⚠️`) in the list.
- See the Performance & Caching guide for strategies to fix N+1.

**N+1 Queries Explained**

N+1 queries occur when your code executes one query to fetch a list of records, and then another query for each record to fetch related data.

**Simple analogy**

Imagine you go to a library and ask: "How many books do you have?" (1 query) The librarian tells you there are 10 books. Then you ask: "What are the titles of each of the 10 books?" ... and you ask that 10 separate times (10 more queries). That's 11 queries total — an N+1 problem.

Shows the shape of `$_SESSION`: every key, with nested arrays rendered as indented lists. To keep secrets out of screenshots and shared snapshots, values are never displayed – each one is replaced by its type, for example `[REDACTED int]` or `[REDACTED string]`.

This is still handy for checking that authentication state, flash messages and user‑specific keys exist when you expect them to. To inspect an actual value, use `dd($_SESSION['key'])`.

Displays performance metrics for the framework's cache system (driven by `Cache::remember()` and `Cache::get()`).

- Hits – number of successful cache lookups
- Misses – number of cache misses (values not found)
- Total Requests – hits + misses
- Hit Ratio – percentage of requests that were hits
- A progress bar visualises the ratio with colour coding:
  - Green – > 70% (healthy)
  - Yellow – 40‑70% (room for improvement)
  - Red – < 40% (cache may be underused or ineffective)

If your application is not using caching, the stats will remain zero – that's expected. See the Caching documentation to add cache to your code.

This tab is powered by a React component (`PerformancePanel`) and provides a high‑level dashboard of your application's performance metrics, all in one place.

- Execution Time – same as the header, with a progress bar scaled to 1000ms
- Memory Usage – current memory peak (MB) with a bar scaled to 16MB
- Database Queries – total query count, scaled to 100 queries
- Cache Hit Ratio – the same cache ratio as the Cache tab
- N+1 Detection – summary of any potential N+1 patterns, with a collapsible detail list
- Route / Controller – shows the matched route (same as Request tab)

This comprehensive tab gives you deep insight into your application's runtime environment, middleware pipeline, and dependency injection container. It is your go‑to for debugging bootstrapping issues, middleware misconfigurations, and circular dependencies.

Displays all environment variables (`$_ENV`) in a sortable table. Any variable whose name looks sensitive (passwords, secrets, tokens, API keys) is fully masked, and secret-shaped values are scrubbed. This is useful for verifying that your `.env` settings are correctly loaded.

Shows every middleware that ran during the request, in the exact order they were executed:

- Type – Global (runs on every request) or Route (assigned to specific routes)
- Class – the middleware class name
- Route – the route path (for route middleware)
- Duration – execution time in milliseconds (colour‑coded: green < 20ms, yellow 20‑50ms, red > 50ms)
- Total Middleware Time – sum of all middleware execution times

This is invaluable for pinpointing slow middleware that might be causing request latency, or for verifying that your middleware stack is correctly ordered.

Visualises the service container's dependency resolution for the current request:

- Service – the resolved class (or interface)
- Duration – time taken to resolve (colour‑coded like middleware)
- Called By – the class that requested this service (helps trace dependencies)
- Status – ✅ Resolved (success) or ⚠️ Circular (if a circular dependency was detected)
- Total Resolve Time – sum of all resolution times

If you see a ⚠️ Circular status, the toolbar will also show the circular chain (e.g., `A → B → C → A`), making it easy to fix. This is particularly useful for debugging complex dependency graphs in large applications.

Pro Tip: The Environment tab is perfect for diagnosing "silent" failures – when a page loads but behaves unexpectedly. Check the middleware order and container resolutions to catch misconfigurations quickly.

In development, when an AI client is configured (see the AI Assistant page), the toolbar adds an Ask AI tab. Type a question about the page you just loaded, or pick one of the suggestions (why is this request slow, are there N+1 queries, what did this request do).

- You review first. Review and ask shows the exact text that would be sent, section by section, and lets you untick parts of it. Nothing leaves your machine until you click Send.
- Masked. The message is built from the request snapshot, so secrets are already replaced by `[REDACTED]`. Headers, session values and the client IP are not included by default.
- Answers are text only. The tab never changes your code. For a request that threw an exception, use Explain and fix on the error page.

The tab only appears when the request was recorded as a snapshot. Turn it off with `debug.assist.enabled = false`.

The toolbar is automatically injected when `APP_ENV` is set to `development`. To disable it in development (e.g., to test raw HTML output), you can temporarily comment out the toolbar injection in `index.php` (around line where `Toolbar` is instantiated).

In production (`APP_ENV=production`), the toolbar is never shown, regardless of the `development` setting. This is a security feature.

The toolbar is designed to be extensible. You can add your own panels by hooking into the `Debug::end()` method and injecting custom data into the `$this->data` array. The React components (`PerformancePanel`, `MemoryProfiler`) are also open to extension.

For advanced use, refer to the source code in `vendor/arout/rhapsody-core/src/Debug.php` and `vendor/arout/rhapsody-core/src/Toolbar.php`.

Happy debugging!

The toolbar is your best friend during development. Use it to catch performance bottlenecks, inefficient queries, middleware misconfigurations, circular dependencies, session anomalies, and request‑level issues before they reach production.
This page lists the most common issues users encounter when working with Rhapsody, along with their solutions. If you run into a problem, check here first.

Symptom: After a major refactor (e.g., moving controllers, changing namespaces, or updating routes), the site works locally but fails on production with a 500 error – even though the code is the same.

Cause: The route cache file (`storage/cache/routes/routes.php`) was generated before the changes and still contains references to old class names or paths. Production loads the cache instead of the dynamic route files.

Fix: Clear the route cache:

```bash
php rhapsody route:clear
# Or manually:
rm -f storage/cache/routes/routes.php
```

After clearing, test the site. Once everything works, you can regenerate the cache:

```bash
php rhapsody route:cache
```

Tip: Always clear the route cache after any change that affects class names, namespaces, or route definitions – especially when deploying to production.

Symptom: Pages work in development but fail in production, often with a 500 error or a message about not being able to write to a directory.

Cause: The web server user does not have write permissions to the `storage/` directory (or subdirectories like `cache/`, `logs/`, or `uploads/`).

Fix: Ensure the web server user has write access. For example:

```bash
chmod -R 755 storage/
chmod -R 755 storage/cache/
chmod -R 755 storage/logs/
# If using uploads:
chmod -R 755 storage/uploads/
```

If the server uses a different user/group, you may need to adjust ownership:

```bash
chown -R www-data:www-data storage/   # (or the appropriate user)
```

Symptom: The application works locally but fails on production with errors about missing database connections, mail settings, or other services.

Cause: The production `.env` file is missing required variables (e.g., `DB_HOST`, `APP_KEY`, etc.).

Fix: Copy your `.env.example` to `.env` and fill in all required values. Common variables to check:

- `APP_ENV=production`
- `APP_URL=...`
- `DB_HOST`, `DB_NAME`, `DB_USER`, `DB_PASS`
- `APP_KEY` – must be a 32‑character string (generate with `php -r "echo bin2hex(random_bytes(16));"`)

Symptom: Changes to Twig templates are not reflected on the site, even after refreshing.

Cause: Twig caches compiled templates in `storage/cache/twig/`.

Fix: Clear the Twig cache:

```bash
rm -rf storage/cache/twig/*
```

Or, if you have the CLI command:

```bash
php rhapsody cache:clear
```

Symptom: The application fails with an error like `Failed opening required '/tmp/__CG__AppEntities...'`.

Cause: Doctrine generates proxy classes for entities, but the proxies are missing or the directory is not writable.

Fix: In production, set `APP_ENV=production` and ensure proxies are pre‑generated:

```bash
php vendor/bin/doctrine orm:generate-proxies
```

Ensure the proxy directory (`storage/cache/doctrine/proxies/`) is writable, or pre‑generate them and commit them.

Symptom: When `VITE_DEV_SERVER=false`, the site loads but styles/scripts are missing, or you get a 500 error.

Cause: The Vite production build has not been run, so `public/build/.vite/manifest.json` is missing.

Fix: Run the production build on the server:

```bash
npm install    # if not already done
npm run build
```

This creates the manifest and the fingerprinted assets. Ensure the paths in `ViteManifest.php` match your setup (default is `public/build/`).

Symptom: The application throws a fatal error like `Class "App\Controllers\SomeController" not found`.

Cause: The namespace does not match the directory structure, or Composer's autoloader has not been refreshed.

Fix:

- Ensure your PSR‑4 mappings in `composer.json` are correct.
- Run `composer dump-autoload -o` (production) or `composer dump-autoload` (development).
- Check that your controller files are in the correct directory and have the correct namespace.

Symptom: The site shows a plain 500 error page with no details, even in development.

Cause: The error handler might be failing, or error reporting is disabled.

Fix:

- Check the PHP error log ( `storage/logs/errors.log` or the server's PHP log).
- Temporarily enable `display_errors` in `index.php` to see the actual exception.
- Check the web server error log (Apache/nginx).

Symptom: Services that should be lazy‑loaded are being instantiated too early, or you get errors about missing proxy classes.

Cause: The lazy loading system uses proxies generated in `storage/cache/proxies/`. If this directory is missing, or if the proxies are outdated, issues may occur.

Fix:

- Ensure `storage/cache/proxies/` exists and is writable.
- Run `php rhapsody build:proxies` to pre‑generate proxies.
- Check that `LAZY_LOADING_ENABLED` is set correctly in `.env`.

Symptom: The home page works, but all other routes return a 404 or 500 error.

Cause: `.htaccess` is missing the rewrite rules, or `RewriteBase` is not set correctly.

Fix:

- Ensure `.htaccess` contains the standard rules:

```apache
RewriteEngine On
RewriteBase /
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-f
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-d
RewriteRule ^ index.php [QSA,L]
```

- If the site is in a subdirectory, set `RewriteBase /subdir/`.
- Also check `APP_BASE_URL` in `.env` – it must match the subdirectory (or be empty if in root).
If your issue isn't listed here, check the official Rhapsody documentation, or open an issue on GitHub with a detailed description of the problem, the steps to reproduce it, and the error logs.
Rhapsody includes a powerful set of console commands to make updating your application simple, safe, and automatic.

The recommended way to update your application is by using the `app:update` command. It orchestrates the entire update workflow to ensure a smooth deployment.

```bash
php rhapsody app:update
```

The command performs the following steps in sequence:

1. Enters Maintenance Mode: Puts the site into maintenance mode to prevent access during the update.
2. Fetches Latest Code: Forcefully resets your local branch to match the remote repository, ensuring all new files (like `.env.example`) are downloaded.
3. Updates Dependencies: Runs `composer install`.
4. Syncs Environment File: Safely appends any new variables from `.env.example` to your `.env` file without overwriting your settings.
5. Runs Database Migrations: Applies any pending schema changes.
6. Clears Caches: Flushes all route and application caches.
7. Updates Version: Updates the `app_version` in your `config.php` file.
8. Exits Maintenance Mode: Brings your application back online.
After pulling the latest framework version, always run `php rhapsody env:sync` to add any new environment variables required by the new version.

If you wrote your own driver implementing `CacheInterface`, update its method signatures to match the interface: `get(string $key, mixed $default = null): mixed` and `put(string $key, mixed $value, int $minutes): void`. A driver that omits the `mixed` return type on `get()` will fail to load. See Caching for the full interface.

The `Rhapsody\Core\Validator` class provides a simple and powerful way to validate incoming data from forms and API requests. It helps ensure data integrity and provides a clean way to handle errors and user feedback.

When validation fails, the controller passes an `errors` object and an `old` object back to the view. You can use these to repopulate the form and display error messages next to the relevant fields. ```php
```

- `required`: The field must not be empty.
- `email`: The field must be a valid email address.
- `url`: The field must be a valid URL.
- `min:X`: The string must be at least X characters long.
- `max:X`: The string must not exceed X characters.
- `confirmed`: The field must have a matching field named `{field}_confirmation` (e.g., `password` and `password_confirmation`).
- `numeric`: The field must be a numeric value.
- `alpha`: The field must consist entirely of letters.
- `alpha_num`: The field must consist entirely of letters and numbers.
- `date_format:Y-m-d`: The field must be a valid date matching the given format.
- `in:foo,bar,...`: The field's value must be in the given list.
- `not_in:foo,bar,...`: The field's value must not be in the given list.
- `image`: The uploaded file must be a valid image (jpg, png, gif, webp).
- `mimes:jpeg,png,...`: The uploaded file must have one of the given MIME types/extensions.

The View layer is responsible for presenting data to the user. Rhapsody uses the powerful Twig templating engine to keep your presentation logic separate from your PHP code. This makes your HTML cleaner, more secure, and easier to manage.

All view files are located in the `views/` directory and use the `.twig` extension.

When you use the `@core` namespace in your templates (e.g., `{{% extends "@core/layouts/main.twig" %}}`), you inherit the framework's default design system.

Framework Styling:

- Tailwind CSS v4.3.2 – The default theme uses Tailwind for all styling.
- Dark mode support – Built-in light/dark/system theme switching.
- Responsive by default – Mobile-first design with Tailwind's utility classes.
- Google Fonts – Montserrat font family is pre-loaded.

chunks.text:
If you want to keep the framework's default styling but add your own custom CSS, you should:

1. Copy the core `main.twig` to your theme:
  ```bash
  cp vendor/arout/rhapsody-core/resources/views/themes/default/layouts/main.twig views/themes/your-theme/layouts/main.twig
  ```
2. Add your custom stylesheets in the `styles` block:
  ```twig
  {% block styles %}
      {# 1. Keep the core Tailwind styles (or replace them) #}
      <link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ base_url }}/css/app.css">
      
      {# 2. Your custom styles #}
      <link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ base_url }}/css/custom.css">
      
      {# 3. Keep the Google Fonts #}
      <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com">
      <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>
      <link href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Montserrat:ital,wght@0,100..900;1,100..900&display=swap" rel="stylesheet">
  {% endblock %}
  ```
3. Create your CSS files in `/public/css/`:
  ```bash
  public/css/app.css
  public/css/custom.css
  ```

💡 Tip:

If you're using a build tool (like Vite or Webpack), you can output your compiled CSS to `/public/css/` and reference it with `{{ base_url }}/css/app.css`.

If you want to completely replace the framework's styling (e.g., use Bootstrap instead of Tailwind):

1. Create a new theme in `views/themes/your-theme/`
2. Create your own `layouts/main.twig` from scratch
3. Set `APP_THEME=your-theme` in your `.env` file

See the Theme Customization guide for more details – new themes must include certain core Twig blocks (e.g. `{% block head %}`, `{% block content %}`, etc.)

The framework automatically makes the following variables available in every Twig template:

Variable | Type | Description
`{{ base_url }}` | string | The full base URL of your application. Use this for all links.
`{{ app_url }}` | string | The APP_URL from your `.env` file.
`{{ app_env }}` | string | The current environment (`development`, `production`, etc.)
`{{ app_theme }}` | string | The active theme name from `APP_THEME` in `.env`.
`{{ auth.check }}` | bool | `true` if a user is logged in, `false` otherwise.
`{{ auth.user }}` | object|null | The logged-in user object (with `name`, `email`, `user_id`, etc.) or `null` if not logged in.
`{{ flash.success }}` | string|null | Success flash message (displayed once, then cleared).
`{{ flash.error }}` | string|null | Error flash message (displayed once, then cleared).
`{{ schema_markup }}` | string | JSON-LD structured data for SEO (rendered at the end of the page).

💡 Additional Variables:

You can also access any data passed from your controller via the second argument to `view()` or `react()`. These are merged into the template's context.

The framework provides several useful Twig functions that you can use in your templates:

Function | Description | Example
`route()` | Generates a URL for a named route with optional parameters. | `{{ route('auth.redirect', {provider: 'facebook'}) }}`
`csrf_field()` | Outputs a hidden input field with a CSRF token. | `{{ csrf_field() }}`
`vite_assets()` | Loads Vite assets (dev server or production build). | `{{ vite_assets('resources/js/app.jsx') }}`
`react_component()` | Embeds a React component as an "island" in a Twig template. | `{{ react_component('UserStats', {userId: 1}) }}`
`captcha_form` (variable) | Raw HTML for a CAPTCHA form (rendered with `|raw` filter). | `{{ captcha_form|raw }}`

The `route()` function generates URLs based on named routes defined in your `routes/web.php` file. This is the preferred way to create links because it keeps your URLs maintainable: ```twig {# Simple route without parameters #} Home {# Route with parameters #} View Profile {# Route with query parameters #} Page 2 ``` 💡 Tip: Named routes are defined in your `routes/web.php` file using the `->name()` method: `$router->get('/profile/{id}', [ProfileController::class, 'show'])->name('profile.show');`

If you have CAPTCHA functionality enabled, the `captcha_form` variable contains the raw HTML for the CAPTCHA widget. Use the `|raw` filter to render it:

```twig
<form method="POST" action="{{ base_url }}/submit">
    {# Render the CAPTCHA widget #}
    {{ captcha_form|raw }}
    
    <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>
```

⚠️ Security Note:

Always use the `|raw` filter when outputting `captcha_form`, as it contains HTML markup that would otherwise be escaped by Twig. Only use `|raw` with trusted content – the framework ensures `captcha_form` is safe.

One of Twig's most powerful features is template inheritance. Instead of repeating your site's header and footer in every file, you can create a base layout and have other templates "extend" it. Our framework uses `views/layouts/main.twig` as the main site template. It contains all the common HTML, including the header, navigation, and footer. ```php
...
{% block content %}{% endblock %}
...
``` A specific page template then extends this layout and provides content only for the `content` block. ```php {# views/home/index.twig #} {% extends "layouts/main.twig" %} {% block content %}

Welcome to the Home Page!

This is the content for our home page.

{% endblock %} ```
